#4793. QuantumScape unveils Osprey all-solid-state cell: 1,000 cycles at 1 atm

QuantumScape (QS) is finally going all-solid-state. Its new Osprey platform swaps the liquid in its cathode for a sulfide solid electrolyte, and the company says the cells have hit 1,000 full cycles to 80% capacity at just one atmosphere of pressure.

That’s a big deal for the sulfide camp, which includes Toyota, Samsung SDI, BYD, and Factorial. Their cells typically need heavy clamping to work. But the white paper behind the announcement shows these are small, early lab cells, and some headline numbers come with important conditions.

Here’s something QuantumScape has rarely spelled out this plainly: its current product isn’t all-solid-state.

The new white paper describes the QSE platform, including the QSE-5 cell it’s shipping as samples from its Eagle Line pilot production in San Jose, as a ceramic separator paired with “a relatively conventional high-nickel NMC cathode and a liquid catholyte.”

The solid part is the separator. It sits between the cathode and a lithium-metal anode that QuantumScape doesn’t manufacture at all. The cell is built “anode-free,” and lithium plates against the separator during the first charge.

Osprey keeps that separator and anode-free design and swaps the liquid in the cathode for a solid sulfide electrolyte. That makes the whole cell solid.

The interesting part is that QuantumScape hasn’t changed its mind on sulfides. It has spent years arguing that sulfide electrolytes can’t work as separators, and the white paper doubles down, calling their problems “fundamental properties” of the material rather than engineering challenges.

The company lists four issues: sulfides react with lithium metal, they need high pressure to keep contact with the electrodes, they struggle at room temperature and below, and they can’t handle fast charging with a lithium-metal anode before dendrites form.

The pressure point is the one automakers care about most. QuantumScape illustrates it this way: 20 atm on a single 10 x 24.2 cm cell works out to roughly 5,000 kg of force, about three mid-size cars. Holding that across a pack takes thick steel end plates and tie rods, which add weight, volume, and cost.

And 20 atm is on the generous side. Many sulfide cells in labs run at 30 to 100+ atm (3 to 12 MPa), and some even higher. China’s FAW reported large-format sulfide cells cycling at 5 MPa, or about 50 atm, in September, which was billed as a low-pressure achievement.

So QS’s pitch is simple: keep the sulfide in the cathode, where it’s good at moving lithium ions, and let the QS ceramic separator handle the lithium metal.

QuantumScape published four main data sets:

This is the strongest result. A 2-layer cell with a 50 x 65 mm cathode, the same area as QSE-5, ran 1,000 cycles to about 80% capacity. The test used full 1C charge and 1C discharge, 0 to 100% state of charge, 30°C, and 1 atm. The cathode loading was 5.5 mAh/cm², which is in line with commercial EV cells.

QuantumScape says no other sulfide-based cell has shown this, and Electrek couldn’t find published data that contradicts it. Academic groups have shown sulfide cells running with little or no external pressure, but not for 1,000 full cycles with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode.

But this is a small cell. By our math, two layers at that size come out to roughly 0.3 to 0.4 Ah, compared to about 5 Ah for a QSE-5.

The press release says “five-minute fast charging from 10% to 80%.” The white paper shows that was achieved at 10C, in a 2-layer cell, at 80°C (176°F). The chart itself is captioned “High temperature enables 5 min fast charge.”

Batteries charge much faster when hot, and EVs do precondition packs before fast charging. Still, 80°C is well above what EV packs are usually preconditioned to before a fast charge. QS didn’t publish a room-temperature fast-charge result.

“Operational down to -20°C” came from a single-layer cell with a 21 x 21 mm cathode, discharged slowly at C/3. It kept 68% of its room-temperature capacity at -20°C (about 52% of its energy) and 85% at 0°C.

That’s a real result for a sulfide system, which have historically needed heat. But it’s a tiny cell at a gentle rate.

The “up to ~1,100 Wh/L” figure is a projection. QS says high-loading cathodes (10 mAh/cm², about double today’s EV cells) are possible with sulfide catholytes. The test backing that up used an 11 mm coin-size cell at 3 atm, not 1 atm, and ran for 100 cycles.

For reference, QSE-5 is rated at 844 Wh/L and 301 Wh/kg.

QuantumScape is pitching Osprey as an “open platform.” Customers can use QS’s own sulfide cathode, made with a proprietary dry process, or bring their own. QS says it has already tested Osprey with solid cathodes developed by its automotive customers.

In other words, after years of being the sulfide skeptic, QuantumScape now wants to sell its separator and anode-free design to the companies that have spent billions developing sulfide cathodes.

That fits the licensing model it already uses with Volkswagen’s PowerCo and Honda. QS reported $9.8 million in customer billings in Q3 and announced a 100 MWh production line targeting start of production in 2028 for QSE-5.

There’s no timeline for Osprey. The white paper says the process has been demonstrated “at laboratory scale,” that higher-throughput processes are “in the development stage,” and that “significant work remains in process engineering.” Automakers also want larger prismatic cells than QSE-5, which means more layers and more area per layer.

Everyone else is on the clock. Samsung SDI is targeting mass production of sulfide all-solid-state cells in its Ulsan plant in the second half of 2027. BYD plans small-batch sulfide solid-state production in 2027, with mass production toward the end of the decade. Toyota is aiming for 2027 to 2028, after slipping from 2020, 2023, and 2026. Factorial’s sulfide Solstice platform is targeting up to 450 Wh/kg.

CATL, the world’s largest battery maker, said in June that true mass-market solid-state is still “years away,” around 2030.

None of those companies has published 1,000-cycle data at 1 atm with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode. That’s QuantumScape’s opening shot.

This is the most interesting thing QuantumScape has published in a while. The numbers are good, but the strategy shift probably stands out most.

The cycle-life result is legit. A 2-layer cell with commercial-area electrodes and realistic loading doing 1,000 full 1C cycles at 1 atm and 30°C is the kind of data the industry hasn’t shown. And QS published the test conditions, which is more than many of its competitors do.

Key thing to remember is that this is a lab test cell. There's a long road ahead to mass manufacturing.

Also, when it hopefully hits the market it will be an incremental improvement, not a quantum leap. Current cells are already in the market doing things like 5 minute charging.

But you can argue the press release oversells what’s in the white paper. A 5-minute charge at 80°C isn’t the same thing as a 5-minute charge, and the release should have said so. The energy density is projected, the cold-weather result is from a cell the size of a postage stamp, and 80% after 1,000 cycles is well below the 95% after 1,000 cycles PowerCo confirmed in QSE’s early cells back in 2024. Different chemistry, different stage, but something worth keeping in mind.

So QuantumScape is essentially admitting the liquid catholyte in QSE isn’t the end game, and that the industry’s massive sulfide investment is something to plug into rather than fight. If your separator is the one part everyone else can’t make work, selling it to them is smart.

The question is time. QS is still scaling QSE-5, with a 100 MWh line not due until 2028. Osprey is a lab process. Will anyone in the sulfide camp license it before their own 2027 to 2030 production plans lock in? At this point, it sounds like this is QS’ bet right now.

If you’re following battery breakthroughs because you want cheaper, cleaner energy at home, the tech that already works is solar plus storage. #4792. A wobbly exoplanet vanished—but astronomers aren’t worried

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 11, 2026 4:01 PM EST

For the first time, astronomers witnessed a gigantic exoplanet dramatically vanish from view. But the “hot Jupiter” located about 1,000 light-years from Earth didn’t evaporate into the vacuum of space. Instead, the gravitational pull from an uncomfortably close neighbor is causing TOI-2535 b to wobble in its orbit thanks to the same dynamics dictating solar and lunar eclipses. The unusual discovery is detailed in a study recently published in Astrophysical Journal Letters, and relies on observations gathered by NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) orbital telescope.

“We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true,” Samuel Yee, a University of California Los Angeles (UCLA) astronomer and study co-author, explained in a recent profile. “If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other’s orbits.”

Astronomers first began examining TOI-2535 b in April 2019 using TESS. The eagle-eyed telescope identifies new planets by flagging subtle changes in stellar brightness. These changes are often caused by a previously unknown planet’s transit in front of its star as seen from Earth. In some ways, TOI-2535 b resembles our solar system’s largest planet, but it is even closer to its own star than Mercury is to our sun. While Mercury takes 88 days to complete the trip, TOI-2535 b circles back around once every 8.25 days.

While using TESS to get glimpses of TOI-2535 b over the next seven years, researchers realized the hot Jupiter’s transits didn’t occur on a regular schedule like most other planets. Instead, the exoplanet’s light fluctuations could arrive upwards of six hours earlier or later than predicted. Over time, astronomers also noticed these transits become shallower and shorter. Then, in March, TOI-2535 b simply didn’t show up during the space telescope’s scan of the system.

Researchers including Yee now believe their hot Jupiter isn’t alone—it actually has an incredibly close gas giant neighbor with a comparatively tilted orbit. The two planets’ relationship causes them to essentially wobble like a pair of tops, eventually throwing one another out of alignment so that they disappear from Earth’s viewpoint.

“This is the most extreme example we’ve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly,” said Yee. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching.”

The forces at play are the same as those that ensure eclipses don’t follow a regularly repeating cycle. UCLA astrophysicist and study co-author Erik Petigura explained that this is due to the moon’s tilted orbit, which comes from its cataclysmic early formation following a collision with Earth.

“If the moon’s orbit around the Earth was perfectly aligned with the Earth’s orbit around the sun, we would see an eclipse every month,” Petigura explained.

Yee, Petigura, and their colleagues are lucky to have spotted TOI-2535’s disappearing act when they did. Based on their calculations, its next transit in front of its star won’t occur for another 30 to 50 years—although they may see its partner planet sooner once it emerges from behind its stellar anchor.

#4790. How to Navigate Seasonal Affective Disorder as a Couple

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

As the weather cools and the leaves begin to change color, another change can occur: The depressed moods that come along with Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD) can begin to arise. SAD can do more than just dampen one’s mood in late fall and winter; it can also negatively impact one’s relationships. As fall arrives, one may want to get out and see the changing leaves, visit a pumpkin patch, or indulge in some holiday shopping. However, their partner may just want to crawl back under the covers and hibernate until the spring. Approximately 5% of people in the United States experience symptoms of SAD as the days grow shorter. Symptoms usually begin to show around mid-fall and carry on through the winter, beginning to relent around spring and summer. When one partner struggles with SAD, it can create feelings of frustration and resentment within the relationship. The fatigue, irritability, social withdrawal, and lack of sexual desire that can come with SAD may change how couples spend time together or interpret one another’s behavior. Here we discuss some practical ways to acknowledge our loved one’s feelings and SAD-related symptoms while still maintaining a connection and making room for how each person approaches the changing seasons.

SAD is officially defined as a major depressive disorder that has a seasonal pattern, following a regular cycle that typically begins and ends at the same time every year. People who experience SAD during the colder fall and winter months can have persistent low moods, low energy, sleepiness, changes in appetite, and a desire to withdraw from social activities.

The symptoms of SAD can be more severe than the “winter blues” that many of us deal with as the days get shorter and it gets darker earlier. For those who grapple with SAD, the activities of daily functioning are disrupted — and this can include their intimate relationships. Before judging a partner too harshly for what may seem to be a sudden mood change that comes as colder weather sets in, perhaps suggest that they meet with a professional to have an assessment done for seasonal affective disorder. Framing it as something psychological rather than assuming that one’s partner has lost interest in the relationship as a whole can help both partners approach the issue more productively.

SAD can have an impact on all aspects of daily life, from getting up in the morning to performance at work to interactions with the ones we love. This can create an imbalance when one partner is dealing with the negative effects of their SAD, and for the other partner, it is business as usual. SAD can lead to a decrease in motivation, which can look like disinterest from the outside looking in. One of the best ways to salvage a relationship when one person has SAD is to prepare before the symptoms set in. Focus on open communication between one another and ask questions such as “What kind of support feels most helpful when you are struggling?” or “How can we best stay connected when your energy is low?” Emphasize listening, sincere reassurance, and respectful communication over trying to solve a problem that may not be immediately solvable. The partner with SAD should come away from discussions feeling like their perspectives, needs, and opinions matter. For couples navigating seasonal depression, there are ways to connect when moods are low. The important thing to remember is to remain flexible. Suggest several options for time together, such as a short walk, a simple meal at home, or an affectionate touch that does not carry the expectation of sex. Be prepared to offer “low-energy” or “high-energy” versions of plans to work around the fluctuating symptoms of SAD. Offer invitations instead of hard and fast plans and try to stay away from statements that suggest the person needs to try harder to “break out of their seasonal funk.” It’s important in the relationship to support the partner with SAD without becoming their therapist. By keeping empathy and communication at the forefront, you can weather the seasonal depression period together.

Even the most well-intentioned partners can’t have all the answers. While keeping to a strategy of empathetic support and simple routines, seeking the advice of a professional can also go a long way in helping people with SAD. Treatment options such as psychotherapy, light therapy, and antidepressant medications can help people withstand the most challenging aspects of SAD until the symptoms begin to lessen as the days grow longer and the weather becomes warmer.

The colder months bring a lot of time for togetherness, from holiday parties to enjoying outdoor adventures in the snow. However, when a couple is navigating seasonal depression, the fall and winter seasons can look different. By sticking with small, flexible ways to stay connected and keeping the lines of communication open, couples can help make the season easier without allowing seasonal depression to define their relationship.

#4789. Genesis reveals GV90 prices start at $100K+ in Korea, but it will cost more for coach doors

Genesis opened orders for the ultra-luxury electric SUV in South Korea, with prices starting at over $100,000. If you want coach doors, however, it will cost you a bit more.

Hyundai’s luxury brand is moving upscale with the GV90, its first fully electric three-row flagship SUV.

After unveiling the GV90 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco in August (which we had the pleasure to see firsthand), Genesis launched the new “ultra-luxe” SUV in its home market of Korea on Tuesday.

The Genesis GV90 introduces several “world-first” innovations, including the first independently opening and closing B-pillarless coach doors, a 12-airbag roof airbag system, and genuine wood floors with radiant heating.

It’s available in two models: the GV90 Standard with traditional swing doors and the GV90 Neolun, which features the “Neolun Arch Gate,” Genesis’ hidden B-pillar coach door system.

In Korea, the Genesis GV90 Standard 7-seater model starts at 139.5 million won, or about $104,000.

The GV90 Individual Lounge Seat (6-seater) starts at 145.5 million won ($108,500); the GV90 Neolun Standard (6-seater) starts at 189.9 million won ($141,500), while the top-spec GV90 Neolun Executive Suite (4-seater) starts at 239.5 million won ($178,500).

Based on Hyundai’s new eMP platform, developed exclusively for its flagships, Genesis said the GV90 is like a “moving private lounge,” complete with a multi-chamber air suspension and a dual electronic limited-slip differential (E-LSD).

The platform is designed to open up interior space for the B-pillarless coach doors, swivel seats, and more.

When parked, the front seats swivel a full 180 degrees to face rear passengers or to create what Genesis calls “a face-to-face lounge-like configuration.”

The interior is about as over-the-top as you could expect, with massive digital screens, premium materials, and plenty of luxury extras.

The GV90 is the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle to feature its new extendable display and the first Genesis model equipped with its next-gen Pleos Connect infotainment system.

Together, they create what Genesis calls a new realm of “display expandability.” While other vehicles, like the new Tucson and IONIQ 3, also use Pleos Connect, Hyundai developed an exclusive version for the GV90.

When the vehicle is parked, the screen can expand to 24.6″ at the push of a button, transforming it into a massive Cinematic Display.

Once extended, the display switches to Media Home mode, where you can watch Netflix, live TV, stream music, and more with third-party apps.

A mobile private theater wouldn’t be complete without a premium audio system, right? To top it off, Genesis added a 25-speaker Bang & Olufsen Premier 3D Sound System with Dolby Atmos, so it sounds like you’re actually at the movies.

In place of a traditional instrument cluster, the GV90 has a 25″ Head-Up Display (HUD) that shows the vehicle’s speed, navigation directions, and other ADAS functions directly on the windshield.

The GV90 is also the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle with a buttonless power system. When you enter the vehicle and close the door, the Motion Column Shifter moves from the 12 o’clock position to the 2 o’clock position.

Meanwhile, the Crystal Sphere between the driver and passenger rotates to indicate it’s ready to drive. The vehicle starts when you press the brake.

As a full-size flagship SUV, the Genesis GV90 is massive. It measures 208.1″ (5,285 mm) long, 79.9″ (2,030 mm) wide, and 71.5″ (1,815 mm) tall (71.4″ with 24″ tires), with a 127.8″ (3,245 mm) wheelbase.

That’s even bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 (199.2″/5,060 mm in length) and Kia EV9 (197.4″/5,010 mm).

To power a full-size flagship SUV, it needs a big battery. The GV90 uses a 123.5 kWh battery, the largest among Hyundai Motor’s EVs, which Genesis said provides a driving range of 500 km (310 miles) for the 7-seater version with 22″ wheels.

The GV90 Neonlun 6-seater with 24″ wheels has a range of up to 460 km (286 miles) on a single charge.

It’s equipped with a new dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) system that delivers a combined 657 hp (490 kW) and 590 lb-ft (800 Nm) of torque, making it Hyundai Motor Group’s most powerful electric vehicle.

When using a 350 kW fast charger, the vehicle’s battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 22 minutes.

And.... once again Hyundai shortchanges the range. If you are going to drop a 200+ inch premium upright SUV into the market it requires a 140+ kwh battery (Rivian, BMW) to deliver segment appropriate range. You do not have to jump to a 200 kwh Escalade (though it is probably a better buy in every respect) but at least deliver 140+. Also, memo to powertrain engineering group: 350 kw is getting outdated on fast charging especially on a vehicle of this size. And while I am at it, what happened to the promised L3 ADAS? I think the 2028 Caddy is worth the wait compared to this.

“Thanks to the enthusiastic interest and support for the GV90 since its global premiere, we have begun full-scale sales in Korea first,” a Genesis official said, adding the flagship SUV will “set a new standard for luxury.”

Following Korea, Genesis is expected to launch the GV90 in the US and other global markets in early 2027.

Genesis has yet to reveal US prices, but the GV90 Standard model is expected to start at around $100,000. The GV90 Neolun, on the other hand, will likely start closer to $150,000 or more.

What do you think of the flagship Genesis GV90? Would you buy the standard version for about $100,000 or pay the extra for the Neolun with coach doors? Let us know in the comments.

#4786. 6 Signs Grand Theft Auto VI Is Coming Between You and Your Partner

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

After 13 years of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) has finally arrived, and many people are signing off from their lives and signing on to the virtual world. Set in the fictional, Florida-inspired state of Leonida, the latest installment takes you through palm-tree-lined streets, lavish estates, neon-lit nightclubs, and alligator-infested swamps. In this world, you can cruise in a sports car listening to a killer soundtrack featuring artists such as Tame Impala, Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott, and PinkPantheress.

The graphics and attention to detail are remarkably realistic, making the experience immersive, even when painting your virtual bedroom in anticipation of your girlfriend coming home from prison.

In the weeks leading up to the release, it has been intriguing to see how frequently the excitement surrounding this game has made its way into my therapy sessions. So many people have talked about taking time off from work and booking hotel rooms so they can play uninterrupted. Many are considering skipping the holidays this year and spending Thanksgiving in Vice City rather than at the dinner table with their families.

As a couples therapist, I find this idea of disappearing into a virtual world fascinating, and to some extent, understand the appeal. Who wouldn't want to check out right now? Between geopolitical tensions and the threat of AI taking people’s jobs, reality hasn't been doing a great job of selling itself lately.

Entering a world where you don't have to worry about grades, respond to your mother's texts about the holidays, or figure out what to make for dinner while accommodating everyone's increasingly complicated dietary restrictions can be appealing. But when does checking out become a problem for your relationship?

Interestingly, at the center of GTA VI is the story of a couple, Jason and Lucia, who rely on one another to survive. Imagine spending hours navigating the complexities of a fictional couple's relationship while neglecting your own.

It’s remarkable how resourceful we become when we truly want something. Couples regularly tell me they’re too busy and too exhausted to plan date nights, weekend getaways, or even small, thoughtful gestures. Yet many of those same people somehow find bandwidth to take days off work, book hotel rooms, and clear their schedule for a video game.

A person may spend six hours tending to their virtual snake and re-stealing a car, but an hour of bedtime for their children feels like a waste of time. In Vice City, they have energy to strategize, learn from their mistakes, and keep trying, but when it comes to being emotionally available for their partner, they're ready to call it a night. Getting their relationship with Lucia from "Running on Empty" to "Hot Together" is worth an entire weekend, but planning an outing with their real partner requires three weeks' notice and a Google Calendar invitation. These are signs that focus on the game is having a negative effect on the real-world relationship.

Part of the appeal is that, in the game, the objectives are clear. Real relationships are messier. There are no YouTube tutorials walking you through every challenge or showing you how other people solved it. Still, if you can devote hours to mastering the complexities of repainting your car, finding new sunglasses, and stashing your weapon, some of that patience and determination can also be made available for the people in your real life.

If your partner is repeatedly calling you for dinner or your children are begging you to come see something they've been building, and these requests feel like inconveniences standing between you and your next engine upgrade, it might be worth examining what's happening.

Fascinating how buying flowers, answering texts, and remembering a girlfriend's preferences can become second nature to a person when a little heart pops up on the screen to celebrate, while managing these things in real life can feel like a difficult challenge.

It's important to remember that one of our most fundamental attachment needs is knowing that we can reach our partner and that they will respond when we need them (Johnson, 2008). When mundane attempts at connection generate responses of irritation or withdrawal, people will eventually learn to stop reaching out. Maybe initially, the peace and quiet can feel like a victory, but eventually, it will get in the way of what we really want, which is meaningful, loving, and connected relationships.

Booking a hotel room to spend three days playing a video game while your spouse drives your kids to soccer practice or plans your family's Thanksgiving meal is not a decision that just concerns you. Being in a committed partnership doesn't require relinquishing your personhood. It does, however, involve recognizing that your choices have consequences for other people.

Creating a couple bubble is about establishing a mutual agreement to protect and prioritize the relationship and look out for each other (Tatkin, 2012). It is healthy to want some space for our hobbies in our relationship, but when our leisure comes at our partner's expense, that will hurt the partnership.

In my practice, I see many couples whose romantic relationships gradually deteriorate into parent-child dynamics. One partner assumes more of the adult responsibilities. They begin monitoring screen time, reminding the other person of their obligations, managing household chores, worrying about their health, keeping track of bedtimes and meals, and making sure someone shows up to pick up the kids.

Meanwhile, the partner being "parented" feels criticized, controlled, micromanaged, and deprived of their freedom. This is not a healthy dynamic between adult partners.

The most alluring part of an alternate reality is that you can leave your emotional baggage behind. You don't have to process grief, worry about your aging parents, or think about the Christmas gifts you can't afford.

You can avoid difficult conversations about whether you're going to get married or try IVF treatment. And of course, unwinding is important to recovery, but before you know it, you can find yourself looking forward to your partner falling asleep so you can finally enjoy your evening by yourself.

You're working tirelessly to get your relationship with Lucia to "Hot Together" while your actual partner is wondering whether filing for divorce would finally unlock your attention.

The desire to escape isn't abnormal or shameful. We're overloaded and overstimulated. Real life is difficult, and our sense of agency is constantly challenged. However, it is valuable to understand what exactly it is that we are running away from.

As much as the desire to retreat into a different reality is understandable, we also could make our actual lives different, but of course, making real-life changes requires being present.

None of this means we can't enjoy the art, music, and unapologetically excessive world that GTA offers. But the real challenge isn't completing another mission; it's figuring out how to bring some of that same excitement, curiosity, and determination back into your relationship.

#4785. Porsche CEO takes a shot at Tesla’s ‘flying’ Roadster stunt show

Tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche. Speaking at a conference in Berlin today, CEO Michael Leiters said Porsche wants “to completely steer clear from any kind of effects and shows,” according to Bloomberg.

Both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15. Tesla made a Roadster flip in mid-air. Porsche showed the Mission S, and Leiters says the two cars aren’t even chasing the same customers.

Tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype. The main event was a car using compressed-air thrusters to launch off a ramp, rotate in the air, and come back down on its wheels.

It was the payoff for months of hype. Musk spent most of the year promising a “flying” Roadster demo, and it slipped more than once. We reported in June that it had been pushed to August to make room for SpaceX thruster work.

There are three versions. The Performance trim uses suction fans and claims 0-60 mph in under 1.6 seconds, the Thrust trim adds rear cold-gas thrusters for a claimed sub-0.9-second run, and the single-seat Rocket trim gets thrusters all around the car and isn’t approved for public roads. Tesla gave no price and no production date, just Musk’s “2028, actually.”

Porsche went the other way. Under the skin, the Mission S can take either a hybrid or a straight combustion powertrain. It’s a mid-engine car that sits above the 911 in the lineup, and well above it in price.

Leiters said customer response has been “overwhelming” and that Porsche would rather show off real technical innovation than put on a show. If it reaches production, Ferrari is the obvious target, and Porsche hasn’t played in that segment since the 918 Spyder. Porsche is counting on a pricier, more exclusive lineup to rebuild its profits.

Not everyone in the supercar world agrees with Leiters. Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna rated Tesla’s Roadster launch “10 out of 10” last month.

Leiters has a point, even if Porsche pitching a gas and hybrid supercar as “technical innovation” in 2026 is a bit rich. But what bothers me more is who Tesla is aiming at.

I’m concerned Tesla is starting to appeal to the lowest common denominator: people who watch a Roadster hop off a ramp and believe an actual flying car is coming. Musk pushed that idea himself. On Joe Rogan’s show, he called the upcoming demo “unforgettable” and said that if Peter Thiel wants a flying car, “we should be able to buy one.”

That’s not real. Cold-gas thrusters work like a giant can of compressed air, and the math is brutal. The Rocket trim carries 400 liters of air at 10,000 psi, roughly 200 kg of gas. At the roughly 80 kN its rear thrusters produce, even a very efficient nozzle empties that tank in a few seconds. Then refilling it takes six to seven hours.

Also someone on Bluesky pointed out that the video shows Mach diamonds in the exhaust stream of the thrusters. Which means it's so loud that anyone within 100 feet would suffer immediate and permanent hearing loss. This Roadster isn't useful for anything other than temporarily pumping stock prices.

So the Roadster’s “flying” will always be limited to stunts like this one. No hopping over traffic. No hovering. A couple of seconds of air, then a long wait at a compressor.

That’s great for a viral clip. But this is a car that dropped from a promised 620 miles of range in 2017 to “over 300” today, and Tesla would rather sell people on a flight the physics can’t deliver.

It’s hard for me to get excited for that. As a BEV enthusiast, I’m not more excited about Porsche’s ICE Mission S, but at least I trust Porsche to actually deliver that to customers.

#4784. Can one intense workout per week keep you healthy? Here’s the science.

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 12, 2026 8:53 AM EST

The so-called “weekend warrior” exercise approach offers an enticing trade: skip the workouts all week, and cram them into one or two days instead. It sounded great to me, until I realized it could turn my hard-earned “Thank God it’s Friday” into “Oh God, it’s Friday.”

Still, for people who genuinely lack the time to exercise during the workweek, this approach could offer real convenience—and real health benefits.

A recent study in Hong Kong has supported that idea, finding that people who packed all their weekly exercise into one high-intensity interval training (HIIT) session lost about as much body fat as those who spread the same workout across three sessions.

So, is doing all your exercise in one session really just as good as spreading it out? The answer depends on your goals and overall health. But according to Dr. Keith Diaz, an exercise physiologist at Columbia University, even infrequent exercise has real value.

“You don’t have to be a daily gym goer to reap the benefits,” he says. “Some exercise, even if it’s just one time a week, provides health benefits.”

The study, published in Nature Communications, spent 16 weeks following 315 adults who were overweight or had central obesity. The researchers split the participants into three groups, with one doing a single 75-minute HIIT session per week, and another spreading this exercise across three weekly sessions.

“They had participants do three 25-minute HIIT sessions of 4 minutes hard and 3 minutes easy,” Diaz says. “There was 15 to 30 minutes between HIIT sessions, plus a 5-minute warm-up and 5-minute cool-down.” The once-weekly group did all three of those 25-minute blocks in a single visit; the second group spread them into three visits across the week, one block per visit. A third group, the controls, did not exercise, and instead attended health education classes.

By the end of the 16 weeks, both HIIT groups had lost more body fat than the control group. Specifically, the once-weekly group lost about 1.75 pounds more than the control group, and the group that exercised three times a week lost 2.2 pounds more. Waist circumference, which is a measure of central obesity, also improved significantly in both exercise groups compared to control.

“These were relatively modest reductions in fat,” Diaz says. Neither group reported any exercise-related injuries.

The researchers measured much more than fat loss. They also tracked cardiorespiratory fitness, which is a measure of how efficiently the body uses oxygen during exercise, and a strong predictor of long-term health.

By this measure, the two workout groups did not perform equally. The group that exercised three times a week achieved roughly an 11 percent improvement in cardiorespiratory fitness, compared with an approximate 6 percent improvement in the once-weekly group. Diaz has a theory for why this might be the case.

“Physiologically, the more frequently you stress your body with exercise, the more it will adapt and yield changes to your heart, blood vessels, and muscles,” he says.

So, if fat loss is your main priority, a “weekend warrior” workout might be enough. However, Diaz believes the study actually makes a case for spreading exercise across the week “if your focus is on being fitter and generally being more healthy.”

So who does stand to benefit from squeezing a week’s worth of exercise into one session? According to Diaz, the ideal “weekend warrior” is a healthy person who, because of the demands of their daily lives, might not get around to exercising otherwise.

“This approach is best suited for generally healthy individuals who are short on time during the week and struggle to exercise because of their busy weekday schedule,” he says.

However, some people with preexisting health conditions might not see the most benefit from this highly consolidated regimen. In particular, Diaz says people with diabetes or hypertension should try to be physically active every day.

“Exercise lowers blood sugar and blood pressure for 12 to 24 hours afterward,” he says. “So, the weekend warrior approach would not be ideally suitable for individuals with diabetes or hypertension, who need these regular reductions in blood sugar or blood pressure.” Diaz adds that people with heart conditions should discuss once-weekly HIIT with their doctors before starting.

Do rage workouts really help to blow off steam?

Should you work out on an empty stomach? Fitness experts weigh in.

How much exercise do I need to stay healthy?

Although the once-weekly approach has undeniable appeal and might truly benefit some busy folks, Diaz notes that it’s not exactly the magical quick fix some headlines would suggest.

“I think the headlines around one day of exercise a week melting belly fat are misleading,” he says. “Yes, it’s one day of exercise, but it’s a lot in one day.”

Although the exercise itself takes 75 minutes in total, adding time to warm up and rest between the sessions means that the single weekly workout takes almost three hours to complete. And it’s not melting the fat away.

Despite that deflating reality check, Diaz sees real potential in this approach when healthy people use it appropriately.

“This study adds further support that some exercise, even if just on the weekend, is better than none,” he says. “So if the weekend is the only time you have to exercise, this could be an option for you.”

#4783. ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they showed little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

Brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is currently no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”

“We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” said Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” said Vaughn.

ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

“I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” said Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

“I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are new or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.

#4782. How Long Should We Wait for Sex, Cohabitation, and Marriage?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

"Wise men say, 'Only fools rush in,' but I can't help falling in love with you." — Elvis Presley

How long should you wait before having sex? Moving in together? Getting married? These are among the most common questions people ask about romantic relationships. Yet there is no magical timeline that guarantees success. The value of waiting depends on the partners, their circumstances, and the nature of their relationship. Still, one principle often proves valuable: patience.

"Patience is not simply the ability to wait. It's how we behave while we're waiting." — Joyce Meyer

There's a crucial distinction between waiting and patience. Waiting is passive: Time passes while little changes. Patience, by contrast, is active. It involves investing in the relationship while recognizing that some developments should not be rushed. Patience creates the conditions for intimacy, trust, and commitment to deepen naturally. Unlike procrastination, which unnecessarily delays action, patience reflects wise timing. The important question is not how long we wait, but whether we practice patience rather than merely let time pass (Ben‐Ze'ev, 2019; and here).

"I don't have a set time frame for sex, but it's always before it gets super serious. I've got to test-drive the car before buying it." — A woman

"My boyfriend and I had sex on the first date, and we're still together a year later and talking about getting engaged soon. The right person isn't going to think less of you because of the speedy sex." — A woman

Sexual attraction is a defining feature of romantic love, making the timing of sexual intimacy especially significant. Research often finds that couples who delay sex report greater relationship quality and lower breakup rates. Waiting may allow emotional intimacy and communication to develop before physical intimacy takes center stage. Some studies suggest that couples who wait several months before becoming sexually involved report greater satisfaction and relationship stability (Vancour & Fallon, 2017).

Yet these findings do not mean that sex on the first date is a mistake. What matters most is not the calendar but the context. Partners differ in their values, attachment styles, and goals. For some well-matched couples, early sexual intimacy may strengthen their initial bond. The important question is therefore not, "How many dates should we wait?" but "Are we both comfortable with the pace at which intimacy is developing?"

"With love and patience, nothing is impossible." — Daisaku Ikeda

Premarital cohabitation has become the norm for most American couples. Yet living together can serve very different purposes.

Research suggests that couples who move in together mainly to "test" the relationship are more likely to break up than those who cohabit because they genuinely want to spend more time together (Chapman et al., 2026). One reason is that living together creates practical and financial interdependence, making it harder to evaluate the relationship objectively. Couples who move in together after discussing long-term plans, or after becoming engaged, generally report better marital outcomes than those who simply drift into cohabitation because it feels convenient.

Researchers therefore distinguish between sliding into cohabitation and deciding to cohabit. Sliding involves little deliberate discussion or commitment; deciding reflects conscious consideration of the relationship's future. Indeed, more than half of cohabiting couples report that they had not explicitly discussed moving in together before doing so. The central issue is not whether couples should live together before marriage, but whether cohabitation expresses mutual commitment and thoughtful deliberation rather than uncertainty and inertia.

"The ideal amount of time to date before getting married is at least a whole year. It's crazy to marry someone before you've seen what they're like in winter." — A woman

No dating duration can guarantee marital success. Nevertheless, many relationship researchers and therapists suggest that two to three years often provides enough time to know a partner across different circumstances while preserving romantic momentum.

Dating typically differs from hooking up because it is part of a broader process of building an enduring relationship. Yet the distinction is far from absolute. Many successful relationships begin as casual encounters. One-night stands sometimes become lifelong partnerships, and dating apps such as Tinder, often criticized for promoting casual sex, have also become important pathways to marriage. The route matters less than what develops along the way.

"Lovers are patient and know that the moon needs time to become full." — Rumi

Love has no universally correct timetable. There are no strict rules governing when to have sex, how long to live together, or how long to date before marriage. What matters is not simply how long partners wait before taking the next step, but whether they use that time wisely. Passive waiting merely allows the clock to advance; active patience allows intimacy, trust, and commitment to deepen. Romantic flourishing depends less on the passage of time than on what partners do with it.

Ben-Ze’ev, A. (2019). The Arc of Love: How our romantic lives change over time. University of Chicago Press.

Chapman, C. L., Liu, D. Y., Stanley, S. M., & Rhoades, G. K. (2026). Thinking about moving in together? Reasons for cohabitation are associated with relationship outcomes over time. Couple and Family Psychology: Research and Practice, 15, 138-151.

Vancour, J. M., & Fallon, M. (2017). Romantic satisfaction in young adults as a function of sexual debut. Psi Chi Journal of Psychological Research, 22(2).‏

#4781. Toyota and Subaru hit the ‘sweet spot’ with affordable electric SUVs

Toyota and Subaru’s new electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.

The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.

Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.

Outside of Rivian, Toyota and Subaru are the only brands that have higher year-over-year EV sales in the US through the third quarter.

Combined, Toyota and Subaru have sold nearly 50,000 EVs through the first nine months of 2026, more than double compared to the same period last year.

Toyota alone has sold nearly 35,000 electric vehicles, up 183.4% YOY, while Subaru sold 14,630, up 46.7%. And that’s not even including the additional 12,676 sold under the Lexus brand, up 137.4% YOY.

While the two Japanese automakers were infamously slow to transition to battery electric vehicles, the timing worked in their favor.

After launching the heavily updated bZ in late 2025, previously called the bZ4X, Toyota’s electric SUV suddenly became one of America’s most popular EVs. Through Q3, it was the fourth best-selling EV in the US, trailing only the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.

Starting at $35,000, the Toyota bZ is one of the most affordable EVs in the US. It also offers up to 314 miles of range in the FWD Plus trim, which starts at $37,980.

Toyota and Subaru now each sell three electric SUVs, which share the same platform and technology.

With prices ranging from roughly $35,000 to about $45,000, Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive, said (via Bloomberg) Toyota and Subaru’s new EVs are affordable and hit the “sweet spot” of the US car market.

Toyota also sells the smaller, sporty C-HR, starting at $37,080, and the larger, more rugged bZ Woodland, which starts at $45,380.

Subaru, on the other hand, sells the updated Solterra ($38,495, plus the smaller Uncharted ($34,995) and midsize Trailseeker ($39,995).

Karla Fisher, a Marine and retired engineer, told Bloomberg that the Subaru Trailseeker was her “most favorite car of all time.”

While she considered buying an EV before the $7,500 federal credit expired last September, none met her requirements at the time. Fisher wanted at least 7″ of ground clearance, 250 miles or more range, and a price that was similar, or even less than a comparible gas-powered vehicle.

The Subaru Trailseeker offers all of that and starts at under $40,000. Toyota and Subaru’s electric SUVs all start at about $45,000 or less, which is even less than the average new vehicle.

According to the latest Kelley Blue Book figures, the average price for a new vehicle in the US reached a record $51,109 in October, up 2.1% YOY.

Great as these may be, there is little inventory to be found.

There are less than 500 Uncharted available Nationwide.

You can't sell what you don't have. Yes, they can be ordered for sure, but how many missed sales does that model create?

Subaru spokesperson Dominick Infante said the affordable EV prices are mainly thanks to its partnership with Toyota. “We do believe there’s an EV future,” Infante added.

Next year, both brands will add a three-row electric SUV with the Toyota Highlander EV and Subaru Getaway.

#4779. Facing Fears in Huntington's Disease

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Every now and then, I get an automated message in my inbox telling me it’s been a while since I’ve tended to my blog:

Dear Pamela Mallette LCPC, It's been 90 days or longer since you last posted to Living With Huntington's Disease on Psychology Today. We miss your voice in the mix.

Too bad, I think. It’s not that I’m trying to be rude, and it’s not that I have nothing to say (ask anyone). It’s just that I look forward to writing about my bad brain about as much as I look forward to sticking my head in a blender.

Don’t get me wrong: I enjoy the writing process. It’s the subject matter that irks me. Being gene-positive for Huntington’s Disease (HD) means I am facing down one of the cruelest diseases known to humankind, and writing about it can be a real downer. There’s a great weight off when I finish a post, and I feel free to live my life without thinking about it again.

But sooner than I’d like, the email comes along, and with it the invitation to return to the matter of my doom. It forces me out of hibernation and into the spasmodic dance between Avoidance and Confrontation: the Death Tango, as I like to call it—fear and courage, in their epic entanglement within my psyche.

Avoidance, in its protective wisdom, tells me to ignore the emails and let the blog go dark. It’s not worth it. It’s too heavy, and you have enough going on. Spend your time on something—anything—else. Not bad advice. After all, there’s no real pressure, no real consequence, if I don’t write.

It feels like safety to avoid. Unfortunately, ignoring it doesn’t get me very far. I can delete an email or neglect a blog, but I can’t erase my DNA. Nor can I ignore the inheritability of this disease (50 percent), which means my children are at risk. Avoidance would leave all of us unprepared for realities to come, and I’m unwilling to do that.

Plus, as a therapist, I know that facing my reality is probably good for me, or whatever.

So I let Confrontation take the lead, if only because there is no other choice. I follow that valorous fool into dangerous territory, where the different faces of HD lurk around dark corners, each triggering their own primal fears within me.

The most common face of HD is chorea, the involuntary, dance-like motor symptoms that take away a person’s physical autonomy. But it goes further. In later stages, HD breaks you down until you are wheelchair-bound, bedridden, and unable to feed, dress, or bathe yourself.

The loss of physical independence is devastating, but that’s not the worst part for me. The world can be a very unkind place for people with physical challenges, and that’s where the fear sets in. Being on the receiving end of ridicule or humiliation when I am defenseless and vulnerable is literally my worst nightmare.

Then there’s the emotional and psychological decline. Because of damage to the caudate nucleus and frontal lobes, behaviors and emotions start to change as the disease progresses. Once caring people become apathetic. Relaxed people become obsessive and demanding. The gentle become irritable and enraged.

What does this mean for me? Am I not going to be funny anymore? Will I be rude to people for no reason? What if I turn into someone I can’t stand? There’s no telling who I will become as the disease progresses, and my soul shudders.

And of course, there’s the death part. It’s not the dying itself that scares me; it’s that HD, that Biological Robber Baron, claims entire decades as it disrupts the natural lifespan. It most commonly manifests during midlife, such that you become incapacitated in your prime adult living years, and often don’t see your golden years at all.

These are significant periods of time that I have been looking forward to. But if my trajectory is typical, I’m not going to have the future I want. Instead, only the stark sorrow that my best days may be already behind me.

So how do I do this? How do I face the darkness without being overcome by it?

Recently someone close to me told me about a memorial service he’d attended. Though he didn’t know the deceased personally, by all accounts the man being mourned lived an incredible life that touched everyone he encountered for the better.

In memorializing her father, his daughter told of a note she found after his death, something he’d scribbled down and posted on a mirror. It had just three words: “purpose without pressure.”

How simple, and how deep, was this man’s wisdom. He didn’t know it, but with those words he was providing my problem with a solution: balance.

Because just as there is fear, there is meaning—purpose—as well. There’s therapeutic value to voicing the fears, because I don’t often speak them aloud (tends to bring down the mood at parties). And of course, there’s the hope that this writing might encourage someone in the HD community, or that it might help those outside the community to have more understanding and empathy.

Perhaps my greatest purpose is this: If HD is going to take my voice from me, then I will use it as long as possible. Where it destroys, I create. I can try to bring some beauty to this journey, even when all I can say is that I hate it and I’m scared.

So yes, I choose to lean into purpose. But because it’s so grave, I heed the advice of the dead. I give myself permission to honor the enormity of the task by taking my time, coming to it only gently, when I am ready. I write from flow, not force, and I release expectation of the outcome.

Thank you, Peter Vlasses. May you rest in your way, and I in mine.

#4778. Hyundai is shaking up its 2027 electric vehicle lineup: Here’s what’s changing

Hyundai’s US electric vehicle lineup will look a bit different in 2027, including the new IONIQ 6 N, a new range-topping IONIQ 9 trim, and a handful of minor updates to the IONIQ 5.

Hyundai announced its 2027 model-year changes on Wednesday, including the new IONIQ 6 N and a few slight changes to the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.

While Hyundai discontinued the standard IONIQ 6, it added the high-performance IONIQ 6 N for the 2027 lineup.

The IONIQ 6 N is Hyundai’s second performance EV, following the IONIQ 5 N. Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the electric sports car delivers a combined 641 hp and 568 lb-ft of torque.

Hyundai said the IONIQ 6 N can sprint from 0 to 60 mph in 3.2 seconds, beating the IONIQ 5 N at 3.25 seconds.

Like the IONIQ 5 N, it also includes fun added features, like N e-Shift and an N Active Sound+ system that simulates the sounds and sensations of a traditional gas-powered sports car with an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission.

It uses an 84 kWh battery that provides up to 245 miles of pure electric driving range. Thanks to its 800V ultra-fast charging architecture, the IONIQ 6 N can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.

Like Hyundai’s other electric vehicles, it comes standard with a native NACS charging port and a CCS adapter.

The 2027 IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are mostly carryover models with a few minor changes, while the IONIQ 5 N remains the same as the 2026 model year.

Changes to the IONIQ 5 for the 2027 model year include roof rails, which are now available on the SEL trim and above; previously, they were only available on the XRT and Limited trims.

Hyundai HomeLink will be available exclusively on the Limited trim, rather than SEL and above, in the current 2026 model year, while the Cargo Cover will be offered as an Accessory only.

Regarding color options, the Gravity Gold Matte and Sage Silver Matte will no longer be available for the 2027 IONIQ 5.

The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250, making it one of the most affordable EVs in the US.

That’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. The extended-range SE RWD model is $2,500 more, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.

Hyundai’s three-row SUV also received a handful of updates. The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 9 will be available with a new Calligraphy Black Ink trim, while the Calligraphy Design will no longer be offered.

The 2027 IONIQ 9 Calligraphy and Calligraphy Black Ink trims gain a Virtual Gear Shift and heated third-row seats. All variants also gain a Tailgate Emergency Lamp.

On the one hand... the Ioniq5 is due for an update. On the other... I still absolutely love the way it looks, and notice just about every one I pass on the road.

Hyundai has yet to announce prices for the 2027 model. The base 2026 IONIQ 9 S starts at $58,995 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 335 miles.

The previous top-spec Performance Calligraphy Design AWD started at $76,490, so you can expect the new Calligraphy Black Ink to be around the same, if not even more.

#4777. Bald eagles Shadow and Kaydee take on a ‘nestoration’ project

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 12, 2026 11:10 AM EST

As nesting season in Big Bear Valley continues, internet-famous bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) father Shadow and his potential new partner Kaydee are putting in the work. Like any couple, the pair is taking on a little “nestoration” project. Kaydee focused on rearranging a few errant sticks and Shadow inspected several parts of the nest.

According to Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV), the nonprofit organization that runs the nest camera, this task looked physically taxing.

“For a short time, Shadow’s tongue could be seen hanging out, a behavior eagles use to help cool themselves,” FOBBV writes. “Since bald eagles do not have sweat glands, they rely on thermoregulation by ‘panting’ to regulate their body temperature.”

The birds then quietly listened to the sounds of the valley, while remaining alert for any potential intruders like the eagle they encountered earlier this week. They managed to chase off that would-be interloper.

Kaydee eventually turned around from her watch, and Shadow showered her with “affectionate little nibbles,” before moving to the front porch of the nest. Shadow stood on the back porch to watch over their territory. They then enjoyed the morning sunshine for over an hour while guarding their home.

Later in the day, Kaydee flew in from a branch called the lookout snag to the nest. When she arrived, she loudly announced her presence before flying off once again. Three other eagles were observed flying across the territory shortly after she left.

“It is encouraging to see Shadow and Kaydee working together to defend their territory while continuing to strengthen their bond,” FOBBV writes. “Watching this devoted pair grow closer with each passing day is truly a joy!”

We still do not know if Shadow and Kaydee will mate this season. Bald eagle nesting begins in September, and lasts over six months. Any eggs are generally laid in January. Viewers can follow Shadow and Kaydee and their journey on the nest via a 24/7 livestream.

Kaydee, formerly known as KD1, is a banded female bald eagle that has been spotted in Big Bear Valley following the death of Shadow’s former partner, Jackie. She was born in 2022, about 70 miles away from Big Bear Lake in the Prado Basin between Anaheim and Riverside, California. Coincidentally, her parents are also named Lucky and Ricky like Jackie’s parents, but they are a different eagle pair.

Kaydee was banded as part of the Orange County Water District’s work to track the eagles born in the area. These bands help biologists track and monitor the birds over time. Kaydee currently has a black spot on her head, but that may not be permanent. It’s possible that not all of her white feathers have come in or it could be tree sap or dirt. She also has two small bands on her legs. One is a small metal band, while the other is a lavender band with “KD1” on it.

Kaydee is almost five years old, so she is just about ready to mate.

In January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers who died from cancer in February.

On July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.

She was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center said that she was in unstable condition on August 9. Her packed cell volume (PCV) fell below percent, before rising to nine percent. Jackie died early in the morning on August 10. The necropsy did not reveal a single cause of death, and instead pointed to several factors including severe anemia, bird flu, blood clots in her wing and one kidney, and liver and lung abnormalities.

A memorial service was held on September 5 in Fawnskin, California, along with a second celebration of life called Wings Over Big Bear on October 3. The event featured representatives from FOBBV, the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, and more.

In November, the Ojai Raptor Center announced a “room filled with kindness,” that is covered with thousands of letters, drawings, cards, and well-wishes they have received in honor of Jackie.

#4776. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”

The fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

GLP-1s are a big topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

The line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She says her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

“I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

But despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

“I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” said Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

“There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she says. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”

Ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”

It’s important to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

One of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.
