#4721. Lunar’s new home DC fast charger puts your EV battery to work

Lunar Energy has unveiled a 25-kW home DC fast charger that will do more than just power up your car really fast. Paired with its next-generation home battery system, the Lunar Fast Charger will also let a compatible EV help keep the house running during an outage and potentially earn money by sending electricity back to the grid.

The new battery system will be available to customers in early 2027, with the charger rollout expected in mid-2027.

Lunar says its home DC fast charger can add roughly 100 miles of range in an hour at up to 25 kW. Actual results will depend on the vehicle and charging conditions.

This is a DC charger, according to Lunar’s product specifications. It connects directly to the DC side of the Lunar Battery, and Lunar says that setup avoids an electrical panel upgrade for the charger. The product page lists CCS and NACS connector support but doesn’t specify which cars will support bidirectional charging.

That distinction matters. Charging an EV and sending power back are separate capabilities, so buyers will need to check vehicle compatibility before relying on home backup.

With a compatible EV, Lunar says vehicle-to-home (V2H) charging could extend backup power through a multi-day outage. How long it lasts will depend on the car’s available battery capacity and what’s running in the house.

Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) payments will also depend on the availability of programs. They aren’t an automatic benefit of installing the charger.

The updated Lunar System has a 13.4 kW inverter and uses 5 kWh battery modules. A single tower holds 10–30 kWh, while towers installed side by side can provide up to 300 kWh.

Lunar is also expanding into small businesses, with pad-mounted configurations reaching 1 MWh. Businesses could use the batteries for backup and to reduce demand charges, or fees tied to their highest power draw.

The system can work with new solar using Lunar Maximizer panel optimizers, existing solar, or no solar at all. Lunar says assembly takes place in California, Georgia, Idaho, and Washington, with engineering and R&D in Mountain View, California.

Lunar AI uses electricity prices, weather forecasts, and a property’s energy use to decide when to charge batteries or supply power. Adding the EV gives it another battery to coordinate with rooftop solar and household battery storage.

The company reports that its California customers using Lunar AI saved an additional $338 on average last year compared with a standard battery operating mode.

Lunar’s Gridshare platform already manages more than 150,000 distributed energy devices worldwide. It groups those resources into virtual power plants (VPPs), allowing utilities and other energy providers to call on stored electricity when demand rises and offer customers incentives for participating. It currently operates VPPs in California, Hawaii, and Texas and is expanding in Utah, Nevada, and New Jersey. It also operates in Europe, the UK, and Japan.

Lunar hasn’t yet disclosed pricing or named compatible bidirectional EV models. Those are two important details homeowners will need before deciding whether this setup makes sense for their driveway.

#4720. Can squirrels really survive any fall?

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 15, 2026 7:54 AM EST

On any ordinary day, you might witness the breathtaking display of squirrels high in the trees, doing what seems like effortless, daredevilish parkour. They might launch themselves off one branch, bounce off another, and somehow reorient themselves in midair like it’s nothing.

A large, heavy human being attempting these same maneuvers would likely fall—and would be looking at a trip to the E.R., at best.

Yet squirrels, it seems, tend to walk away from these situations unscathed. You’ve probably even heard that squirrels can survive a fall from any height. But according to Dr. Nathaniel Hunt of the University of Nebraska at Omaha, this comes with an important caveat: Even these brazen little gymnasts don’t stick the landing every single time.

“I would put an asterisk on the claim that squirrels can survive a fall from literally any height,” Hunt tells Popular Science. “Their size makes large falls surprisingly survivable, but they are not invulnerable.”

So, can squirrels survive, if not all, most falls? And if so, how?

It’s much more than luck that keeps squirrels landing safely; they are no more immune than we are to the laws of gravity. It’s what happens in the air—both in terms of their anatomical engineering and their instincts—that allows them to survive most falls and get right back to their nut-hiding hijinks.

According to Hunt, a falling squirrel faces three challenges: the speed of the fall, its orientation midair, and the impact when it lands. A squirrel’s small body helps; at about a pound, a squirrel weighs about as much as a loaf of bread.

“Being small gives it a lot of aerodynamic area relative to its weight, so air resistance limits its speed,” Hunt says. “It also has much less kinetic energy than a larger animal.”

So, squirrels’ light and small bodies help them hit the ground with less force, but that’s not all that’s going on. Hunt says squirrels instinctively know how to move through the air and land on the ground, which helps to optimize their already “favorable physics.” The tail is a key player in these midair maneuvers.

“The tail is more interesting than a fluffy parachute,” Hunt notes. “At low airspeeds, aerodynamic forces are small, but the squirrel can still use inertial tail movements to exchange angular momentum with the body and control orientation.” In other words, squirrels use their tail to control how and where they fall.

Research backs Hunt’s claim. A 2021 study found that squirrels experiencing unexpected falls were able to rapidly rotate their tails, a motion that caused the rest of their bodies to rotate in the opposite direction. Hunt compared the role of the tail to that of a “reaction wheel” on a spacecraft.

“Accelerating the tail in one direction helps rotate or stabilize the body in the other direction,” Hunt says.

As a squirrel’s fall picks up speed, the tail may function more like the feathers on an arrow, Hunt suggests. If the squirrel starts to veer off course, the airflow pushes against the tail just enough to redirect its body into a stable position. Even then, the tail isn’t acting like a true parachute; instead of slowing the squirrel’s descent, the tail is nudging its body in the right direction.

Size, anatomy, and aerial reorientation are all important to a squirrel’s seemingly magical ability to survive most falls. However, there’s a third skill that plays an equally important part, one Hunt thinks may be “the most underappreciated part of the story.” Squirrels know how to come in for a landing.

“A recent study I co-authored found that fox squirrels managed more than 80 percent of their landing energy through their forelimbs,” Hunt says of a study looking at squirrels leaping between branches. “They also adjusted their forces depending on whether they undershot or overshot the branch.”

In other words, a landing isn’t just something that happens to a squirrel. On some level, they’re doing damage control.

“They are not simply hitting the branch,” Hunt says. “They are actively controlling the collision.”

So, how slowly does a squirrel have to fall to be able to walk away?

The answer lies in our furry friend’s terminal velocity, the top speed something reaches while falling once air resistance balances gravity’s pull and stops it from accelerating further. Hunt says a squirrel’s terminal velocity can be reasonably estimated at about 20 to 40 mph, depending on its posture, limb position, and tail. For reference, Hunt estimates the terminal velocity of a cat—famous nine lives aside—at about 60 mph, while a belly-down human skydiver is likely to fall at about 120 mph.

“All of these are approximate, because posture matters enormously,” he says.

Posture explains some of the variation, but size is ultimately the main driver. A giant squirrel, therefore, would likely fare much worse in a fall, even with perfect tail control and posture.

“You could not simply build a squirrel 10 times larger and expect it to tolerate the same fall,” Hunt says.

Likewise, a squirrel’s comparatively slow terminal velocity doesn’t mean it’s out of the proverbial woods. It might seem that once a squirrel hits its maximum speed, height wouldn’t matter much, making a fall from 10 feet and a fall from 100 feet equally survivable. Hunt cautions against assumptions like this.

“Reaching terminal velocity does not make a squirrel immune to injury,” he says. “The landing surface, body orientation, and any collisions along the way still matter.”

This complex interplay of physics, instinct, learning, and split-second decision-making is part of what makes squirrels a fascinating study subject for Hunt.

“What fascinates me is that you cannot neatly separate ‘the brain’ from ‘the mechanics,'” Hunt says. “Squirrel agility emerges from sensing, learning, body shape, and physical dynamics working together.”

#4719. BYD wins round one in Defender-copycat battle as JLR is told to destroy documents

BYD just got some good news in its Defender-copycat court battle with JLR. After JLR had BYD’s Netherlands offices raided and documents seized, a Dutch court has now handed BYD an early win, ordering JLR to destroy the documents or face a penalty.

After BYD opened orders for the Ti 7 in Europe and the UK in late July, many (including us at Electrek) compared it to the iconic Land Rover Defender, with its boxy, rugged (yet still elegant) SUV design.

BYD even described it as having “an unapologetically boxy profile” that delivers “the imposing, chunky design that finds favour among SUV buyers, yet delivers a contemporary look.”

In August, authorities on behalf of the British luxury automaker raided BYD’s offices in the Netherlands without prior warning and seized digital records.

On November 11, a Dutch court in The Hague ruled against JLR and ordered the company to destroy the seized documents, which included launch plans and other technical data, so they wouldn’t fall into anyone else’s hands.

JLR must destroy the documents within 24 hours of the ruling or face a fine of €50,000 ($55,000) for every hour it is delayed, with a maximum penalty of up to €500,000 ($553,000).

Within 24 hours of destroying it, JLR must also provide BYD with third-party confirmation that it has been destroyed. The court also rejected the British automaker’s request to pay a €500,000 ($553,000) fine.

According to Autoweek Netherlands, the ruling is based on the fact that JLR doesn’t need the documents, noting that the Ti 7 has not yet been sold in the European Union.

BYD won the ruling, and JLR is prohibited from taking any further legal action under the initial seizure order, but JLR has already begun summary proceedings over the infringement in Rotterdam and The Hague.

JLR claims that the Ti 7 SUV is a “slavish imitation” and infringes on the intellectual property of the Land Rover Defender and that BYD stripped down the Defender to reverse-engineer some of its technology.

Before the raid, BYD claims it fully cooperated with JLR’s requests. BYD’s lawyers called the British automakers’ raid a “fishing expedition” and claimed that “too many files were seized.”

The Ti 7 is on sale starting at £47,995 ($64,000) in the UK, on the road. That’s over £20,000 ($26,500) less than the plug-in Defender 110, which starts at £71,840 ($95,500) in the UK.

It has a seven-seat arrangement, which BYD said was specifically designed for the European and UK markets.

As the first vehicle in the UK based on its DM-p (Dual Mode performance) powertrain, BYD said the Ti 7 “vastly exceeds the closest competition,” seemingly another jab at the Defender.

"JLR believes BYD stripped down the Defender to reverse engineer some of its technology"

Reverse engineering isn't illegal. Patent infringement is illegal.

Competition strip down each other's product all the time. As long as they don't use the "exact" same technology, it isn't a copy right issue.

The setup uses three electric motors and a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine, delivering a combined 402 hp (408 PS), enabling it to accelerate from 0 to 62 mph in 4.8 seconds.

The engine primarily powers a 35.6 kWh BYD Blade Battery, which provides a pure-electric WLTP driving range of up to 74 miles. In the city, it has an electric range of up to 102 miles.

Available exclusively in the UK in the flagship Excellence AWD trim, BYD claims that the Ti 7 offers “a level of equipment that exceeds anything that its rivals can offer at this price point.”

We should learn more about the BYD and JLR legal battle soon. Check back for updates, as this story is still ongoing.

#4718. Scientists created artificial, life-like muscles for humanoid robots

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 15, 2026 11:15 AM EST

For better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities. They’ve already experimented with stretching lab-grown human skin over robot faces and with a synthetic hydrogel skin that lets robots really “feel” burns and cuts. Now, a team of engineers at the University of Pennsylvania wants to dig under the skin. In a  study published this week in Advanced Functional Materials, the team describes a highly controllable artificial robot muscle inspired by the small muscles in human eyes and fingers. They put them to the test by having a robot hand strike piano keys at varying intensities and made a set of human eye muscles able to maintain a gaze. It all feels quite uncomfortably adjacent to the 1973 sci-fi film and HBO series Westworld.

Designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat. For starters, most large robots today, especially humanoid ones, rely on bulky, rigid motors and components. That’s fine for more straightforward actions like walking and lifting, but recreating the muscles that move our eyes or fingers requires far more delicate precision. In this case, the engineers needed a material that prioritized flexibility and fine control while staying strong enough to hold up after repeated use. As with many aspects of robotics, tasks that seem quite easy for humans to do are actually often the most difficult tasks for machines. While bipedal robots have been pulling off dance routines and performing acrobatics worth of a Marvel superhero for years, they still fall flat when it comes to something as simple as folding laundry or holding a gaze.

“Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang said in a statement.

For their muscle fiber, the team settled on liquid crystal elastomers (LCE) combined with graphene and an embedded ultrathin copper coil. The LCE, a rubber-like material, acts as the actual muscle, both contracting and stretching. The graphene serves as a reinforcer, making the material both a bit softer and tougher, so it holds up even when opposing muscles pull in other directions.  Together, these two ingredients can produce movement, but on their own they struggle to stay put. When heated, the LCE stretches but then keeps contracting, eventually creeping back toward its original length as it rapidly cools. That’s a problem for subtle movements like holding a gaze or pressing a piano key with light, steady force, where the muscle needs to hold a precise position over a period of time.

That’s where the coil comes in. The team added the coil inside the fiber to serve as a kind of temperature gauge, and the sensors determine when the muscle is losing heat and contracting. With those readings, the team could then gradually increase temperature to ensure the muscle held its position.

“We used the resistance of the embedded copper coil as a feedback signal and adjusted the heating power in real time to keep the resistance near a target value,” added study co-author and University of Pennsylvania Ph.D. student Xuelin Wu. “Because the coil served as both a heater and a sensor, we did not need a separate sensor for feedback.”

With their artificial muscle designed, it was time to test it in real-world scenarios. First, the team fitted the muscles into a 3D-printed robot hand built to mimic finger movement.  They then made the fingers press various piano keys at different levels of force and speed. Sensors placed on the bottom of the keys were able to tell how hard each note was played. The detached hand was no Mozart, but it worked.

Next, they mounted a pair of robotic eyeballs on freely rotating ball joints inside 3D-printed shells. The muscle fibers were attached around the edges of opposing pairs, which were meant to mimic how muscles in the eyes stretch and contract. In testing, the eyes shifted their gaze on demand, with controlled, repeatable movements. The resulting video demonstration is both impressive and unsettling.

The research joins a growing field of labs and companies racing to build artificial muscle systems. In 2025, Polish startup Clone Robotics took the idea to an extreme with a horrifying video of a faceless, human-sized robot dangling from a ceiling and writhing, its movements supposedly powered by synthetic muscles and a hydraulic system meant to mimic human muscles and blood vessels. They call  their creation the world’s first “musculoskeletal android.” Though it is likely that their video was more a shocking proof-of-concept than an actively working prototype, it nonetheless provides a glimpse into a potentially unsettling future where robots replace mechanical motors and actuators with more human-like muscle fibers.

Protoclone, the world's first bipedal, musculoskeletal android. pic.twitter.com/oIV1yaMSyE

The University of Pennsylvania researchers say the next step is combining more of these muscles into larger, integrated systems, where dozens of small muscles have to work together to produce more natural expressions. Down the line, they’re interested in potentially using AI computer vision to coordinate those into even more complex systems. Authenticity is the point. The long-term goal, they note, is to create robots that look and feel more and more like the real thing.

“I’m excited about the possibility of using this approach to create robots that move with the same subtlety and expressiveness we see in human faces,” concluded University of Pennsylvania engineer and paper co-author Ziyun Zhang.

#4717. sonnen’s new smart breakers help your home battery last longer

A home battery can do more during a blackout if it isn’t busy running nonessential, energy-hungry appliances. sonnen and SOLRITE Energy are putting that same principle to work for the grid, adding smart breakers that can temporarily switch off selected household loads while batteries help meet electricity demand.

The companies announced today that they’re integrating ADAPT Energy’s controls and Eaton AbleEdge smart breakers into the SOLRITE–sonnen virtual power plant (VPP). The setup combines sonnenHub with breakers that manage power-hungry equipment, both during outages and when the grid needs help.

The announcement doesn’t specify pricing, how many homes will receive it, or when existing customers can get it.

A VPP connects home batteries into a network so they can work together as a larger energy resource. This addition gives SOLRITE another way to respond: in addition to controlling the batteries, it can reduce the amount of electricity that participating homes use.

sonnen and SOLRITE used the example of a pool pump, as it’s energy-intensive, nonessential, and runs for longer periods. When an event begins, ADAPT temporarily switches off the pool pump while the sonnen battery sends electricity to the grid.

With less battery power going toward the pump, more can flow to the grid. Across participating homes, that gives the VPP more flexibility than relying on battery dispatch alone.

Homeowners have to opt in to that grid participation, and ADAPT will switch off only pre-approved household loads. Joining the VPP program doesn’t give the operator blanket permission to turn off anything in the house.

“Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired, and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home,” said Troy Morgan, president of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy.

The breakers also tackle a practical problem with home backup: Big appliances can drain a battery quickly, and the surge of power some equipment needs to start can overload a backup system just as an outage begins.

ADAPT coordinates the smart breakers with the sonnen battery to automatically switch off large loads during backup operation. When grid power returns, it restores them, so homeowners don’t have to go around resetting individual circuits.

That also gives homeowners more flexibility later. According to the companies, changing which smart-breaker-controlled loads are switched off during an outage doesn’t require rewiring those circuits.

The installation benefit matters, too. Some backup setups require electricians to move selected circuits into a separate panel. This system manages compatible circuits where their breakers already sit, which the companies say reduces installation complexity and inspection work.

Whole-home backup still has limits. Automatically managing large loads helps the available battery capacity go further; it doesn’t mean every appliance can run at once throughout an outage.

SOLRITE finances, builds, and owns residential solar-plus-storage projects through what it calls Virtual Power Plant Agreements, with no upfront cost to homeowners. It says it operates in Texas, California, Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Illinois, with more markets planned.

#4716. The mysterious golden shipwreck that led to decades of lawsuits

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 15, 2026 2:08 PM EST

Long before the Titanic, the most famous shipwreck in the US was the SS Central America. The wooden steamship helped connect San Francisco with New York City before the construction of a coast-to-coast rail network, and sank off the coast of South Carolina in 1857.

425 people died. Most people today haven’t heard of it.

That loss of life alone should be reason enough for people to remember the ship. But the SS Central America was also hauling $1.2 million worth of gold, according to a 1992 court case about the wreck. Given the current value of gold, that’s around $236 million in today’s dollars. And that’s just what’s documented: the ship had a number of wealthy passengers, who were likely carrying their own gold, so the total could be even higher.

A ship full of gold, sunk and lost for over a century. It’s odd that the ship isn’t a household name. And the story keeps getting weirder: the wreck contributed to a massive recession, and when treasure hunters found the ship in the 1980s, decades of lawsuits followed.

Say you wanted to get from San Francisco to New York City in the 1850s. Going over land was miserable—cars were a half century away, and there weren’t many roads. There wasn’t even a rail line connecting the two coasts. Your best bet was to take a ship down to what is now Panama, a train across that narrow bit of land, and then another ship up to New York.

The SS Central America served the Atlantic part of that journey. It left the east coast of Panama on September 3, 1857, with 592 people on board. The ship had one other stop: Havana, Cuba. By September 8, when the ship was leaving that port, the weather looked great, according to a writeup by the US Naval Institute.

That changed—hurricane-force winds battered the wooden hull. By September 11, the crew was working to bail out the ship, and by noon every man joined them. It wasn’t enough: by 2pm the water reached the boilers, leaving the ship drifting. The bailing continued all night, and for a while it seemed like the weather would clear up long enough for a full evacuation. It wasn’t to be—the storm resumed by mid-morning. The captain signaled a nearby ship, the Marine, for help. Only 100 people—including the 59 women and children—boarded the Marine.

The captain went down with the ship around 8pm local time, along with most of the remaining men, who were pulled in by the undertow of the sinking ship. The few men who survived did so by grabbing doors, chairs, and anything else still floating, until another ship—the Ellen—could find them. In total, 425 people lost their lives.

The human cost was high, but there was also a huge economic fallout. A 1992 paper by Lawrence D. Stone, the researcher whose work led to the rediscovery of the wreck, states that the gold on board was intended to shore up several banks already on the brink of collapse. Within a month, almost all banks in the US stopped offering gold in exchange for paper money.

Naturally, a ship this famous—with this much gold on board—became a bit of a legend. Countless people attempted to find the wreck, but no one succeeded until the Columbus-America Discovery Group of Ohio found the wreck in the 1980s. The crew was led by treasure hunter Tommy Gregory Thompson.

The discovery happened thanks to advanced technology—sonar and state-of-the-art remote-controlled submarines. But also because of math.

Stone, whose work I mentioned earlier, explained his method in a 1992 paper. He employed Bayesian search theory. This method begins with finding hypotheses about where the wreck may be, judging how likely each theory is, and ultimately making a map outlining the probability of the ship being in various areas. A route for the search is designed to start with the highest probability areas, continuing from there to lower probabilities.

The survey took 40 days, covering 1,400 square miles of ocean off the Carolina coast. The wreck ended up being in a relatively low probability area, though one included in the route. In 1988, a remotely operated vehicle provided a view of the wreck.

“The storybook result would have been for the Central America to have been found in a high probability area near the beginning of the search,” wrote Stone. “Given the actual result, what can we say about the value of the procedures for developing the search plan? The most obvious thing to say is that they worked.”

That’s the thing about probability: the most likely thing isn’t always what’s true. That doesn’t mean it’s not worth calculating—it can still lead to good results.

But what about the gold? Over the next few years the team brought up most of the commercial gold shipment. A federal judge put its bullion value at about $21 million in 1993, but coins and ingots from a famous shipwreck are worth far more to collectors. In 2000, the bulk of it sold for about $50 million. Today most of the gold is in the hands of private collectors.

This would normally be where the story ends: the treasure is found, the treasure hunters get paid, and everyone is happy. That’s not what happened this time.

By 1989, the insurance companies that covered the SS Central America back in the 1850s argued that the gold belonged to them. Their logic: We paid damages to clients who lost the gold, therefore it’s ours. The insurance companies lost that lawsuit, but it was only the beginning.

Thompson took $12.5 million from investors to fund the treasure hunt. Those investors sued in 2005, alleging they never got any proceeds from the treasure, even after the 2000 sale of the gold. Several members of Thompson’s crew sued in 2006. Thompson went into hiding in 2012, only to be arrested in 2015. He wasn’t released until March of 2026. Some 500 gold coins remain unaccounted for.

It’s an odd footnote to a fascinating story of history, math, and science. And who knows? Maybe this story will still be going a hundred years in the future.

And there may be more to the story of the SS Central America. A 2018 expedition recovered more gold from a safe on the ship, in a passenger compartment. There could be more down there.

#4715. Review: Engwe’s M20 3.0 is a 60V Super73 killer at a fraction of the price

Engwe has impressed us repeatedly with its value e-bikes at lower-than-believable prices. But lately, the brand is climbing the value chain with impressive e-bikes that aren’t just great value but also pack strong specs and impressive features. The Engwe M20 3.0 is a great example…

The Engwe M20 3.0 is a specs monster and blows away the original version of the bike released in 2023:

The M20 is fairly easy to assemble. At just over 100lbs, it is a bit hard to move around, but once assembled, it feels like a pretty impressive piece of machinery. I love the street tires on here instead of pretending to be an off-roader. Dual bright headlights and brake light with turn signals really give this thing some street cred. Adding to the safety roster, Engwe upgraded the quad-piston brakes with sporty red calipers and 202 mm rotors. This is not a value bike. The rear suspension is tight, which is great for 2 riders but might feel stiff out of the box for light riders. The seat is *chef’s kiss* even for 2 riders. Very soft and comfortable but not too soft. It even has a little ‘gas tank’ storage area aft the seat, which is keyed and enough to hold a few sandwiches, some riding gloves, or a small purse.

One gripe: There are 3 sets of keys on here, the aforementioned storage area and one set each for each battery. We’d love to see these things keyed together.

The bike/moped/moto came with a huge 1.2 kW battery (or 2 in our case – unless you have a 80-mile commute, 1 should be plenty) that must be charged individually. But with a 60V 8A charger, each one only takes about 2-3 hours to charge, which is impressive.

I did not expect to like the ride of this thing as much as I did. We can dispense with the pleasantries here; it came set to Class 2 mode with a 20mph top speed and stickers to match; a quick Google search will show you how to open this up to 40mph open mode. I take responsibility for my own actions.

The first thing you’ll notice here is that the motor is whisper-quiet, and with the street tires, there is very little road noise, even at 35mph. The half throttle is plenty responsive, a lot more so than the cadence sensor on the pedals, which are vestigial at best here. Those big brakes are a bit softer than I’d prefer, but given a good squeeze, those 203mm rotors and quad-piston hydraulic brakes are going to stop you, the 100lb bike, and your passenger/cargo fairly quickly.

My girlfriend and I got pulled over for the first time in my e-biking life as I was picking her up at the coffee shop. The cop was immediately apologetic because “he thought we were kids” and not the 50-year-olds under the helmets he encountered. Then he noticed the pedals and said that we’re all clear and that what we were on looked like a motorcycle and that a couple of e-moto kids had gotten into accidents recently, one hit by a drunk driver and who is still in a coma. While he was already letting us go, I pointed out the Class 2 sticker on the bike, and he gave me the thumbs-up as we sped off at 30mph. This M20 passed the local police test with flying colors. I can’t guarantee you’ll have the same experience in your jurisdiction.

Most of my gripes on this e-bike are inherent to the form factor. It is heavy at over 100 lbs, but you’d expect that with a 3.3kW motor, 2.4kW of batteries, and room for two. That said, don’t buy this bike if you need to take it up stairs or plan to pedal it without assist. In fact, this isn’t a bikepath bike or a put it on the back of your car bike. And, don’t buy this bike if you like to pedal. It’s too big and fast. This is a 35 mph roads bike. Also 3 sets of keys?

I did not expect to love this bike as much as I have. It is the perfect train station bike for me, and as a bonus, it is a great way to take my girlfriend to the coffee shop on the weekends. It has fat tires, great suspension, a cushy seat, and strong, smooth acceleration and confidence-inspiring braking. It looks cool enough for the cops to think I’m a kid picking up his girlfriend, and it has so much range that I probably won’t need to charge it monthly. At $1399-$1699 (10% off) depending on battery config, this is less than half the price of some of the pricier and admittedly more stylish Super73 options out there.

I understand that some will fault Engwe for selling a 3.3kW motor e-bike as a class 2 e-bike. But I genuinely feel safer on the road, being able to go at the 35mph speed that cars are going rather than forcing them to go around me. Plus, it isn’t like every single car on the road goes over the speed limit. So why not bikes too?

The Engwe M20 3.0 is over the limit but in all of the best possible ways.

The shoes are designed so the heel compresses as you slip your foot in, then springs back into place (up to 30,000 times a pair). And they’re comfortable from Day One, thanks to the breathable stretch-knit upper (or soft leather on the Vegas 2), insole, and rocker sole/high-rebound midsole, which helps as you rush through a connection or explore a city. So go ahead, kick those shoes off when the seatbelt sign goes off.

The $149 Purple Harmony Anywhere Pillow is for those who are picky about where they rest their head while counting Z’s, whether it’s in a hotel, on a friend’s couch, or while roughing it outdoors. The pillow packs luxury in a compact size: the Honeycomb GelFlex Grid and Talalay latex core keep the pillow firm and cool, while giving plenty of neck support. A moisture-wicking mesh cover keeps things airy, because a hot pillow makes for unhappy travels. Need something more targeted for those long hours in 32C? The Purple Back Pillow is great for portable lumbar support, and has made multiple overnight flights more bearable for us.

Plane cabins and train cars can get chilly; the $90 Rumpl Travel Puffy Blanket balances warmth and comfort with packability. In fact, it’s almost as large as a throw blanket and packs down to the size of a 32-ounce water bottle (shown above for perspective, but not included). Even better, it easily clips onto a backpack. Choose from sunset-inspired shades or your favorite solid color to show off your style while keeping cozy.

These $359 Bose QuietComfort Headphones make an excellent, practical gift and are essential for travel: Planes and trains can be noisy, and playing your media sans headphones is a party foul on every mode of transportation. Bose makes some of the best noise-canceling headphones for airplane travel, from over-ear models to true wireless earbuds. This updated model comes with pill-shaped earcups, a 24-hour battery life, Immersive Audio, QuietControl noise cancellation that mutes practically all outside sound, and updated ActiveSense Tech to smooth sound spikes in Aware Mode.

Not everyone likes big over-ear headphones (like the Bose above), or the feeling and more limited battery life of true wireless earbuds. Well, Marshall has a solution: The $229 on-ear Milton A.N.C. Bluetooth 6.0 headphones, which bring active noise cancellation to a less typical form factor. Six microphones feed the adaptive noise canceling, which is surprisingly effective despite not having the benefit of a complete seal around the ear. Plus, a charge lasts 50 hours with ANC on, and 15 minutes plugged in can get you 9.5 hours more, so New York to Singapore and back ain’t a thang. And adaptive loudness/EQ/spatial audio settings help give those days in the air even more vibes. There’s a USB-C-to-3.5mm cable for wired listening (just remember your seatback entertainment system adapter, and to have the headphones charged because they don’t run passively). They fold up and only weigh 200 grams, so they’re perfect in an already-stuffed personal item, maybe even a jacket pocket. And they’ve got that classic Marshall cool, all textured, leather-like vinyl with brass logo/control knobs. You’ll be rockin’ even when you’re not walkin’ …

We haven’t met wireless earbuds that haven’t announced “battery low” at some point before a flight ended, which isn’t optimal, especially if an attempt at getting some sleep is involved. But these $99 Bose wired earbuds will never give you up, never let you down, never get run down and desert you. Run off the USB-C port of any smartphone, tablet, or laptop, these bring back a newtro style Bose hasn’t made in a decade. And they are unlikely to discontinue it again anytime soon, considering the overwhelming positive response. Using the proprietary QuietControl algorithms that make other Sound By Bose products so good, they cut most perceived noise while providing a convenient three-button in-line remote that switches between Quiet, Aware, and off modes, plus offers playback controls. Plus, multiple eartip-and-stability band size combinations ensure a secure fit. And even if one comes loose on the way in/out of the included case, the 4.2-foot cable means you won’t have that moment of terror that an earbud rolled three rows back.

This $80 Anker Universal Charger combines compatibility with outlets from more than 200 countries into one power block charger. It detects local voltage in one second and is Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory (NRTL)-certified for safe, stable charging. Unlike other international outlet adapters, this one is 25% smaller and designed to stay securely plugged in. And its USB-C/USB-A ports can charge four devices at once, including tech that requires higher voltage, like laptops and tablets.

No outlet is guaranteed in this world, but Anker’s $135 Laptop Power Bank keeps your devices charged when a place to plug in is nowhere to be found. Although it’s branded as a laptop power bank, it can also charge headphones, phones, handheld gaming devices, and more. It can charge an iPhone to full battery at least three times before running empty. The power hub can charge four devices at once. Two built-in USB-C cables mean you won’t have to root around for a charging cable when you need to recharge your tech. It also has a USB-A and USB-C port if you have a proprietary charger for a specific device.

Physical books can be clunky while traveling, especially as a voracious reader. The $160 Rakuten Kobo Clara is a black-and-white eReader that comes ad-free from the jump. I personally prefer it to the Amazon Kindle (which will cost you $170 to go ad-free) for this reason. The Rakuten Kobo Clara BW has 16 GB of storage and can carry up to 12,000 eBooks or 75 audiobooks. An optional Dark Mode makes for better nighttime or dark cabin reading, while ComfortLight PRO adjusts brightness, color temperature, and blue light to help you sleep easier while traveling.

This $80 JBL Clip 5 portable speaker packs pro sound into a pint-sized package. I always bring a small speaker like this one when I’m traveling so I can bump my getting-ready playlist from something that’s more powerful than my phone speakers. Pack it into a personal item or carry-on, or attach it to your person with an improved carabiner clip that sports a wider opening. The JBL Clip 5 has 12 hours of playtime on a single charge, is waterproof and dustproof, and can connect to other JBL Auracast-enabled speakers to get the party started when the plane lands.

Capture travels, adventures, and precious moments in high fidelity with the $700 Insta360 X6 8K Camera. Dual custom-built Sony 1/1.1″ square sensors, a 4-nanometer AI chip that can make edits of your day’s adventures while you sleep, and two imaging chips create quality images and video that feel just like the IRL moment, and 140 minutes of battery runtime keeps the camera rolling for every moment on the itinerary. Built-in stabilization, windproof microphones, and waterproofing up to 65 feet help you capture all the action, wherever it is. This travel gift is excellent for the travel vlogger and adventure enthusiast who records trips for friends, family, and followers to enjoy.

#4712. Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

The risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:

Over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

Previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study showed a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who currently smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he said.

#4711. How much trash is on the moon? About 412,000 pounds.

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 16, 2026 8:49 AM EST

Since the Soviet Union’s Luna 2 probe crashed into the moon’s surface in 1959, the first-ever human-made object to reach the moon, humanity has racked up over 140 missions to our only natural satellite. These missions have delivered 12 humans, seven lunar rovers, and 412,000 pounds (187,000 kilograms) of discarded materials to the moon’s surface. That’s the weight of a Boeing 747 passenger plane.

But these leftovers aren’t all space junk. In fact, some of this debris may prove useful for future lunar exploration.

A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.

Early moon exploration missions, like NASA’s Apollo missions, would land on the moon using a non-reusable lunar module, says Cowley. “It would land, and then the top part of that module would return back to lunar orbit to rendezvous with the command module and return back to Earth. So, the base part of this vehicle would remain.”

Leftover lunar rovers—manned or unmanned land vehicles used to explore the moon’s surface—also contribute to the growing mass of junk. These include China’s robotic Yutu rover, which sent information back to Earth for 31 months, as well as those that crash-landed, like the United Arab Emirates’s Rashid rover.

Other trash on the moon includes scientific equipment, toolboxes, and lunar impactor probes. These are devices that smash into the moon’s surface, not by accident, but to fulfill specific objectives, like close-up imaging or to fire rocks and dust into the air for analysis.

Images of the moon’s barren landscape might make you think that these lunar leftovers simply sit around undisturbed until the visit of the next crewed mission. But that’s not the case.

The moon is an incredibly harsh environment. It’s “constantly bombarded with micrometeorites,” explains Cowley. These tiny rock chunks, along with intense radiation, sunlight exposure, and dramatic temperature swings, will steadily wear down and damage objects.

The iconic American flag planted on the moon by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin in 1969, for example, has likely been bleached almost white by the sun.

But some of this damaged, degraded material could still have value for future moon exploration. Cowley says samples of human equipment on the moon could be assessed to understand how the environment alters them.

Studying the impact of micrometeorites on equipment, for example, “might allow us to produce better solar cell or solar panel protection, so they don’t get degraded for humans when humans may eventually live on the moon,” says Cowley.

In 1960, scientists predicted the world would end on November 13, 2026

Why can’t we just launch all of Earth’s garbage into the sun?

What happens to your body when you die in space?

What would happen if Yellowstone’s ‘supervolcano’ erupted today?

Is turbulence really like Jell-O? Pilots weigh in.

Ahead of plans by NASA and the China National Space Agency to send crewed missions to the moon in the next five years, more equipment will likely amass on the lunar surface. But there are reasons to think these future missions may leave less of a mess behind.

“You might see more emphasis these days on vehicles that have a reusable aspect,” says Cowley. “Maybe the lander can land as one unit and take off as one unit again,” he says. Spaceships in development like SpaceX’s Starship Human Landing System (HLS) plan to adopt this reusable design.

Even if more equipment doesn’t accumulate on the moon, Cowley says the ESA has made plans to reuse some of this moon trash. One project has explored the potential of 3D printing methods to incorporate lunar scrap into new materials. Such efforts will have to account for the likelihood that such materials will be contaminated by lunar dust—sharp, shard-like particles of the rocky lunar surface that can prove a further hazard to machinery.

Cowley says that the lightweight aluminum that makes up the shell of many lunar vehicles could be melted down using concentrated sunlight.

“Rather than bringing things here with you or mining them on the moon,” says Cowley, “you could actually just reuse the old equipment in the same way we recycle stuff down here on Earth.”

That lunar “junk” may prove invaluable to the first humans to one day call the moon home. Or, as the old saying goes, one person’s trash is another person’s treasure.

#4710. Mercedes’s New Tesla-Style Point-to-Point Drive Pilot System Is Useful But Not Quite Convincing

The ‘Level 2++’ system was hesitant and sometimes confused. It still navigated San Francisco for an hour with minimal intervention.

Sitting in the leftmost of two left-turn lanes in a new Mercedes-Benz GLC EV, I notice something strange. I can see my right turn signal on in the reflection of the car in front of me. Then I see my left signal, then my right again. This is less than a mile into an hour testing a new “Level 2++” ADAS system set to be launched by Mercedes, and I have ceded control to what seems to be a hesitant computer that seems to be second-guessing itself.

Thankfully, the visible indecision turns into the right choice. The system turns left from the lane, continues on its planned route, and eventually takes a right a quarter-mile later as it had originally intended.

After the drive, a Mercedes engineer told Road & Track that this could have been a result of disagreement between the priorities of two different systems that go into the MB.Drive-branded point-to-point navigation system. Since the Mercedes ADAS suite uses both the Alpamayo AI model built by Mercedes autonomy partner Nvidia and a “classical stack” of more hard-coded priorities, the engineer inferred that the signal interaction could have been a result of a disagreement between the systems.

The engineer reckoned that the system was trying to think ahead, with the best way to plan for a future right turn being to be in the rightmost of the two left turn lanes. Hence the sudden desire to go one over—a point of conflict. Sometimes, he said, the classical path and the end-to-end model end up in conflict. A more cynical take? That our new robot overlords are already fighting each other.

The interaction was a particularly odd experience in San Francisco. I work in the city and encounter more advanced self-driving pilot programs from companies like Zoox and Waymo every day. Seeing a Waymo Ojai van in traffic at the same stoplight, I thought about how the “Level 2++” Mercedes system seems to be far off the cutting edge being explored at the global hub of automated taxi development.

Fortunately, that turn-signal confusion never came up again. For the most part, the GLC navigated the busy and often unpredictable streets of San Francisco just before evening rush hour without any need for intervention. I actually deactivated the system just once, to take control the first time I came across a widely parked car in a corner. I otherwise trusted it to figure out everything from jaywalkers to chicanes made of two separate double-parked cars a hundred or so feet apart on opposite sides of a tight road. If I had come across the same parking issue later in the drive, I would have trusted the system without taking over.

Other than the confusion at that first intersection, most of my frustrations with the system came from its combination of cautiousness and aggression. Overly-patient ADAS programming is certainly not a bad thing, but I was regularly met with confusion by motorists at stop signs who wondered why the car took so long to get going after coming to a complete stop.

The system’s decision-making with pedestrians would usually be similarly cautious, as it was when the car slowed for someone waiting for a light to cross well within the bounds of a sidewalk. That person was kicking in the air, something that I inferred the car would pick up as a sign that they might start walking soon, so I let the system make its incorrect guess and slowed from around 35 mph to about 10 mph.

Calculations about pedestrians were not always cautious, though. A few miles later, the system opted to enter an intersection while a slower pedestrian crossed after the light turned green. It came surprisingly close to the pedestrian, still well within a safe distance but nearer than I would have driven personally. This felt a bit unnerving with the car’s high beltline and relatively low visibility over the front fenders, but I never came close enough to have to slam on the brakes and take complete control back.

This is a hands-on system that Mercedes still describes as Level 2 autonomy, even if their 2++ designation obfuscates that fact. It is not true autonomous driving, so I followed the guidelines and kept my hands on the wheel and eyes on the road. The closest comparison is Tesla’s absurdly named Full Self-Driving. When this launches, Mercedes hopes to be among the first legacy automakers to directly rival the younger EV brands in this space.

In addition to the headlining point-to-point navigation system, Mercedes allowed us to test a forthcoming hands-free ADAS system available for on-highway use in an S-class and again in a GLE crossover. Unlike the city-driving component, this system allows drivers to completely disengage their hands and feet. It still requires eyes on the road and will aggressively chirp at you to get your hands back on the wheel if you spend too long adjusting a passenger-side mirror. I learned that lesson firsthand, the only time the system forced me to get my eyes back on the road in about 30 miles of highway testing over the two different cars.

This system felt little different from the usual MB.Drive-branded adaptive cruise control. I took control once on this stretch, when the GLE test car signaled to enter a middle lane that a Ram 2500 with a massive trailer was already signaling to enter from the other lane. The system would probably have figured out its own mistake before this became a problem, but I disengaged it entirely and overrode the lane change before I found out how long that would take.

While both systems are temporarily coming for free to select Mercedes models in California as part of an early-access program in December, final pricing and a nationwide rollout for either system remain to be determined. Hands-free highway assist is planned to reach consumers in spring of next year, available to cars on the MB.OS platform with the existing MB.Drive Assist option package.

Point-to-point navigation, the Tesla-style system for in-city driving, will be available as a subscription model. Mercedes says it is coming to cars operating on the brand’s most modern MB.OS-branded architecture starting at some point in 2027. We know that it will be available as a three-year subscription from the factory and in one-year or one-month increments from the car’s digital storefront. Pricing has not been finalized, but a representative from the company claims that it will be “competitive” with comparable offerings from brands like Tesla.

For buyers who prioritize tech that are already looking at one of the products that will be getting the new ADAS suite, the Mercedes system should be worth the eventual subscription price. Given the subscription-only offering and cautious nature of the point-to-point offering, buyers content to drive themselves around a city for a few more years will not be missing out if they opt to forego the new service.

#4709. Zonveer ZX3 review: one of the best-value electric dirt bikes for beginners

The Zonveer ZX3 is one of the best values I’ve seen in electric off-road riding, and one of the most fun things I’ve ridden to date – value for the dollar. Its Black Friday sale brings the 2,800W electric dirt bike down to $1,299, $500 off its $1,799 list price.

For that money, you get a 1,200Wh battery, dual hydraulic disc brakes, and full suspension in a 130 lb package. That’s a great entry point for beginners.

Zonveer is a young brand. It launched in the US in March with two bikes, the kid-sized DX1 and the ZX3, and it’s run by United Mobility, which lists its address in Dover, Delaware. It sells direct and ships from US warehouses, and Zonveer also sells the ZX3 across Europe under its own brand through its EU store.

Here’s what the ZX3 brings, according to Zonveer’s product page:

A hub motor means there’s no motor chain to maintain, and the NFC card and PIN unlock mean there’s no app to fight with. I like that.

Zonveer sent me a ZX3 to test, and I’m impressed with what they shipped, knowing the cost. It isn’t trying to be a race bike. And it doesn’t need to be. Here’s my first ride review:

With 2,800W peak, it’s somewhat modest by e-moto standards. That’s exactly what makes it approachable for someone who has never ridden a dirt bike: the power is enough to have a blast on trails without being intimidating.

My girlfriend had never ridden a dirt bike before, and she got comfortable within a few minutes, and she was hooked as soon as she got the hang of it.

And while testing with my girlfriend, it was clear this bike makes the most sense for lighter riders. Zonveer claims it climbs slopes of up to 30 degrees, which is optimistic for anyone over ~175 lbs, like myself. It still climbed some of the worst slopes on my land, but it did so with some difficulty, which wasn’t the case for some of my lighter friends who also rode it.

Range is the other claim to take with a grain of salt. Riding 45 miles on 1,200Wh means using under 27Wh per mile, which is e-bike efficiency on a 130 lb dirt bike with knobby tires. It’s still a lot of energy, and you can ride this long distances at lower speeds. Just expect less if you ride it hard, and that’s where the fun is at.

Zonveer’s Black Friday sale has the ZX3 at $1,299, and the company gave Electrek readers the code ELECTREK for an extra 5% off, which brings it down to $1,234.05.

The sale also includes a free water bottle and lock, and can be combined for a two-pack of ZX3s for $2,599. Shipping is free, the warranty is one year, Zonveer told us it accepts returns within 30 days on bikes ridden less than 10 miles, with a $200 restocking fee. Here’s the full refund policy.

We’ve ridden a lot of electric two-wheelers, and the ZX3 is one of the most fun per dollar. At $1,299, or about $1,234 with our code, it’s hard to find another 1,200Wh electric dirt bike with dual hydraulic disc brakes and full suspension from a brand that ships from US warehouses.

It’s not fast by e-moto standards, and the range and climbing claims are optimistic. But for beginners, and especially lighter riders, the power lands right in that sweet spot of manageable fun. It’s a bike you can learn on without scaring yourself, and it’s cheap enough that a family can buy two for less than one Sur-Ron.

#4708. 9 rescued orangutans returned to the wild in Indonesia

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 16, 2026 11:06 AM EST

The Indonesian province of West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, is no stranger to wildfires. Horrific wildfires burned in 2015 and 2019, the latter of which set ablaze around 1.6 million hectares of Indonesian forest and land. However, the scale of destruction from this year’s El Niño-intensified fires throughout the island is unprecedented, according to the nonprofit International Animal Rescue.

Earlier this year, four mother-baby orangutan pairs and one adult female orangutan (genus Pongo) were rescued from areas in Ketapang (a regency in the West Kalimantan province) impacted by the fires. They were dehydrated and malnourished, and some had burned their feet, likely because they stepped on embers as they crossed burning peatland.

They were taken to an orangutan rescue and rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, West Kalimantan. The center is run by Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI), a nonprofit dedicated to primate and habitat conservation in Indonesia. YIARI’s medical team kept an eye on their recovery, and then conducted health examinations to make sure they were all ready for release. The last of these examinations revealed that three of the females were pregnant.

“Their return to the wild is therefore especially important, giving these mothers the opportunity to raise their future young in a safer forest habitat,” International Animal Rescue, YIARI’s founding partner, wrote in a statement.

Experts ultimately chose to release them at Batu Nyambu Protected Forest. While also in West Kalimantan, its roughly 23,000 hectares of land and nearby forests haven’t been affected by the recent fires. Batu Nyambu has plenty of natural food, fresh water, nesting trees, and space. But getting the females and their babies there wasn’t simple—they had to travel by road, boat, and on foot for a total of 12 hours. Luckily, they had support from local communities and traditional leaders.

“We are grateful for the support of the community, village governments and traditional leaders,” said Argitoe Ranting, YIARI’s Director of Operations. “The long-term success of conservation efforts depends not only on protecting the area, but also on the role of the people living around the forest in safeguarding habitat and preventing various threats to wildlife.”

Most fires in Indonesia are associated with human activity such as using fire to clear land for plantations and agriculture.

#4707. Mercedes-Benz Is Bringing Tesla-Like Semi-Autonomous Driving Systems to America

Hands-off highway driving and subscription-only hands-on point-to-point navigation are arriving first as part of a California pilot program.

Three years ago, Mercedes-Benz rolled out the first Level 3 autonomy system offered in the United States. That system is no longer available in the latest revision to the S-Class, with CTO Jörg Burzer calling it “early.” The brand still has advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) ambitions, though, and two new major products are arriving for a few customers starting next year. Mercedes-Benz has announced plans to launch both hands-free highway driving and hands-on point-to-point navigation in 2027, part of a continuing partnership with (scandal-laden) semiconductor superpower Nvidia. The latter system is subscription-only, although pricing for that subscription has yet to be revealed.

The hands-free system is limited to “eligible roads,” effectively making it a specialized feature for freeway use. It works up to 85 miles per hour, allowing a driver to take their hands off all inputs while the system handles highway driving and decision-making under the driver’s active supervision. Point-to-point navigation, on the other hand, is a hands-on system with more freedom. Like Tesla or Rivian’s similar offerings, it is intended to handle most of the workload of city driving and react in real time to the peculiarities of that task.

While both systems reach closer to true autonomous driving, their designation as SAE Level 2 systems mean that they are still nowhere near complete autonomy. That label means that they are meant to be seen as driver assistance systems only, leaving the person in the driver’s seat ultimately responsible for intervening before a problem occurs. The same is true of every autonomous solution currently on offer, including systems marketed as “Full Self-Driving” by Tesla.

Some California residents will receive the opportunity to try both systems starting in December; hands-free driving is expected to reach eligible cars more broadly in spring of 2027, while point-to-point navigation is made available nationwide at some point during the next year. Subscription pricing has not yet been announced, but brand representatives have suggested to Road & Track that it will be “competitive” with similar offerings from other automakers.

Mercedes allowed outlets, including Road & Track, to test both systems in San Francisco ahead of the news. You can read more about how the new ADAS offerings fared here.

#4706. Tesla kills $41,990 Model Y AWD: all-wheel drive now costs $8,000 more

Tesla has pulled the $41,990 Model Y All-Wheel Drive from its US online configurator. The cheapest dual-motor Model Y you can order now is the Model Y Premium AWD at $49,990, an $8,000 jump.

The trim lasted just over nine months. Tesla launched it in early February, and it’s gone without a word from the company.

Here’s what Tesla’s US Model Y design studio lists as of today (prices before the destination fee):

When Tesla launched the base Model Y AWD in February, it was basically the stripped-down Model Y with a second motor. It had 294 miles of range, did 0-60 mph in 4.6 seconds and kept the same cut-down cabin as the base RWD. At a $2,000 premium over the single-motor version, it was the most sensible AWD pricing Tesla had offered in years.

And the AWD trim isn’t the only change. In February, the Premium RWD cost $44,990 and the Premium AWD cost $48,990. Both are now $1,000 higher.

Add it up and the cheapest all-wheel-drive Model Y went from $41,990 to $49,990 in nine months. That’s a 19% increase.

The timing isn’t great for Tesla’s competitive position. Chevrolet’s 2027 Equinox EV LT 1 AWD starts at $40,295 before destination, with 307 miles of EPA range. Ford’s Mustang Mach-E Select AWD starts at $40,795.

Both now undercut Tesla’s cheapest AWD crossover by more than $9,000.

If you live somewhere it snows and you were shopping for a new Model Y, the math just got a lot worse. You can still find some base AWD units in Tesla’s inventory, but once those are gone, that’s it.

This is also the latest cut in a year of Tesla shrinking its lineup. Elon Musk killed the Model S and Model X in January to free up Fremont for Optimus, and Cybertruck production is winding down. Meanwhile, the most recent new Tesla is the $61,990 Model Y L, which sits at the top of the range, not the bottom.

We liked this trim. It was the first time in a long time that Tesla treated all-wheel drive as a $2,000 option rather than a huge upsell bundled with a nicer interior, and it put the Model Y right in the price bracket of the Equinox EV and Mach-E with AWD.

Now it’s gone, and the Premium trims went up $1,000 on top of that. Tesla didn’t explain either move. It rarely does anymore.

There are two plausible reasons. Either Tesla is tight on Model Y build slots and would rather fill them with higher-margin Premium trims, or the cheap AWD simply wasn’t selling. We don’t know which. But both explanations land in the same place for buyers: a more expensive Model Y.

Tesla is not going to keep 6 different model Y trims especially when the most expensive trim in the Model YL is selling. They will definitely squeeze out as much money from selling more expensive trims so the lowest end trim will most likely be next to go.

And Tesla has a habit of this. The “Standard” name for its cheaper Model Y and Model 3 lasted a few months. The single-motor Cybertruck, the only version that made sense, was gone within days. Cheaper trims show up, get a news cycle, and quietly disappear.

That’s a problem for a company whose consumer lineup is shrinking down to two cars. The Model Y is Tesla’s volume. Thinning it out at the bottom is the opposite of what you’d do if growing EV sales were the priority.

How long before the $39,990 RWD goes the same way?

#4704. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember. We started with the likes of “Goodnight Batcave” and the lesser-known-in-the-US but oh-so-wonderful collection of verse-driven classics from former UK Children’s Laureate Julia Donaldson.

We moved on to B.J. Novak’s anarchic love letter to the power of words (and to great typography), “The Book With No Pictures.”

We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.

When my eldest, Amelia, hit 6, it was time to roll out the big guns.

Over the last 5 years (she’s now 11), I’ve read the seven Harry Potter books aloud twice, complete with all the voices: once to Amelia on her own, once to both her and her brother, Henry, two years her junior.

I had feared she wouldn’t be keen on another helping, but Amelia immersed herself once more in the world of Hogwarts with no hesitation and took immense joy in watching Henry discover for himself every twist and turn on Harry’s journey.

We have done the same thing with Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” and his fantasy masterpiece “The Lord of the Rings,” and are currently midway through “The Two Towers” on our second go around.

There’s a huge amount of reciprocal joy we take from this nightly ritual, beyond the practical benefits of providing a calming demarcation between the end of the day and the wind-down to sleep.

For me, it comes as either a break in my working day or a signal that it’s over, depending on how hectic things are.

For the kids, it’s an all-too-rare chance to get me all to themselves, no deadlines, screens, or other distractions to pull me away from being anything but 100% present.

For all three of us, it’s a literal (and literary!) warm blanket — a chance to escape under the covers to familiar worlds and familiar faces. It is, in short, incredibly good for our well-being.

And yet, in the world of health information — including on this site — thousands, if not millions, of reading hours are dedicated to the benefits of nutrition, sleep, and exercise as the building blocks of good health. Reading itself rarely makes that shortlist.

For me, it unequivocally deserves a place on it. Research seems to support that case. Even if we need more of it to really understand how and why.

A recent editorial in Psychological Medicine co-authored by Barbara Sahakian, Professor of Clinical Neuropsychology at Cambridge University, draws on a broad range of research linking reading for pleasure to better mental health and greater empathy.

The positive impact of reading on young people — just like Amelia and Henry — also carries evidence.

Among more than 10,000 US adolescents, those who started reading for pleasure early had fewer mental health problems, spent less time on screens and slept more. Although, per an earlier column of mine, I can’t vouch for the sleep side of things when it comes to early bird Henry.

For many, reading can be a form of therapy that improves well-being. Bibliotherapy is a complementary therapeutic tool for emotional release and reduced stress and anxiety, with its roots traced back to ancient civilizations.

There’s even research suggesting a link between a love of reading and a lower risk of cognitive decline.

In a 2003 study of people aged 75 and over, reading was associated with a 35% lower risk of dementia over roughly five years.

A separate 14-year study from 2022 found that people who read at least weekly saw less cognitive decline, whatever their level of education.

A happy (and healthy) by-product of this love of being read to is that both my kids have now started reading to me at bedtime. Henry recently read “Jeffy the Burglar’s Cat” to us, a lesser-known but no less compelling chapter book by Ursula Moray Williams that was a staple of my own childhood. And we’ve enjoyed several books from Amelia, including the wistful tale of friendship and the circle of life, “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White – not a dry eye in the house for the final few chapters of that one.

They’ve also gone off and re-read the Harry Potter books and “The Hobbit” to themselves.

The research above links reading to many health benefits: better attention and memory, fewer mental health problems, more sleep, less time on screens, and greater empathy. I haven’t measured any of those impacts empirically in our house. Nor am I naive to the fact that as they get older, they’ll ultimately grow out of me reading to them, with school, extracurricular activities, their friends, and inevitably screens competing for more and more of their time.

Come what may, though, I know that a child who considers missing a reading session as the most cardinal of cardinal sins, and who scrambles for the chance to read aloud to their dad at bedtime is, at that moment, concentrating, empathizing, discovering and growing.

Researchers are clear that studies espousing the benefits of reading show association rather than proof, and it’s evident that more experimental work and deeper research are needed to ensure the complex cause and effect stands on firm scientific ground.

Regardless, it’s a healthy habit Amelia, Henry and I are very happy to keep, and with a bit of luck, I’ll get to pass it on to their kids one day.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4703. Spider-bear? Black cub wins the 2026 Cutest Climber Award.

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 16, 2026 12:15 PM EST

They may be small, but bear cubs have a pretty steep learning curve. In Alaska, brown bear (Ursus americanus) cubs have a roughly 50 percent survival rate within their first year, while the black bear (Ursus americanus) cub survival rate can range from 51 to 88 percent, depending on where they live. Cubs must learn how to fish, forage, find shelter, and climb trees to escape predators. Fortunately, biology helps out a bit with climbing. Bears have claws that curve and help them go up the tree and then back down safely.

One baby black bear who spent time at Anan Creek in southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest showed off those climbing chops in style. The park’s rangers have officially awarded this bear with the 2026 Cutest Climber Award.

“This little cub slipped on his way down but caught himself and hustled right after mom,” the rangers write. “An adorable reminder that even when you lose your footing, you can recover and keep going. A tiny, furry lesson in resilience provided by the bears of Anan.”

Tongass National Forest’s rangers  are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for tourists on Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Similar to  their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

Revealed via a post on BMW Classic’s Instagram and brought to broader attention to BMWBlog, the video gives us our first look ever at this performance sedan that never was. Conceived in the late 1990s, this 7-Series started life out as a 1997 BMW 740i; BMW then swapped in the 4.9-liter naturally aspirated V-8 from the E39 M5, imbuing it with 400 horsepower.

Not only does it have the M5’s engine, but BMW also paired the motor with a six-speed manual transmission. BMW says the M7 Prototype has a top speed of 155 mph and weighs 4134 pounds. Unfortunately, that’s when the details begin to fall off, and we’re left to observe—or guess—any other info.

Being an M7 Prototype, we suspect BMW went all-out in its M endeavors. That would mean a far sportier chassis alongside larger wheels and tires. This prototype is fitted with BBS wheels, giving it a notably more aggressive stance and look than your typical 740i. The car’s design itself remains understated, making sure to maintain its 7-Series elegance; that said, the rear bumper is modified to make room for the quad exhaust tips you’d see poking out the rear of the E39 M5. No 7-Series from this era featured such an outwardly aggressive exhaust exit, making it one of the few standout exterior changes to this car.

BMW also upholstered the interior with a classy tan and black two-tone. The six-speed shifter is integrated cleanly with the center console. It has a three-spoke M steering wheel, and the cluster is an M unit borrowed from the E39 M5 as well. Suffice it to say, we’re a little sad the company never brought this to production.

#4701. Meta to deploy 25 electric semi trucks across I-10 corridor, but has nothing to ship

Electric truck operator Nevoya is expanding its deal with Meta with the fresh deployment of 25 Class 8 battery-electric trucks on the Interstate 10 (I-10) between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona … but Meta won’t be shipping any products.

The second major trucking deal between Facebook parent company Meta and electric truck operator Nevoya will put 25 new battery-electric semis on I-10, running freight between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona. But Meta isn’t buying trucks, hiring drivers or shipping its own products. Instead, Zuck’s company helping pay for someone else’s cleaner freight through environmental attribute certificates (EACs), a carbon credit mechanism that lets companies claim the emissions benefits of electric trucking without operating the trucks themselves.

“Coming back to Nevoya for a second corridor reflects what we look for in our value chain work: partners that can scale, and agreements we can repeat, said Devon Lake, Head of Net Zero Strategy, Meta. “Freight is part of the emissions footprint of building and operating our data centers, and multi-year commitments like this help address our scope 3 emissions and make electric trucking available and competitive on the routes that serve the regions where we build.”

Meta was one of several buyers in the DC-based Center for Green Market Activation (GMA) buyers’ alliance. The group’s collective EAC purchases supported Nevoya’s initial 63-truck deployment on the Houston–Dallas corridor back in May. This new Agreement, however, is a standalone deal between Nevoya and Meta only, and gives Meta an established framework to open more electric truck corridors in the future.

This clever application of these agreements is what makes the Dallas-Houston run stand out, with GMA calling it, “the first large-scale application of book and claim to zero-emission trucking.” The company adds that this arrangement helps client companies overcome existing barriers to EV adoption while enabling Nevoya to deploy new trucks, “where they deliver the strongest commercial and operational value.”
